subject: Docker & Containers
summary: Containers are the packaging and isolation layer that nearly every modern deployment sits on, and the whole subject rests on one fact: a container is not a small virtual machine, it is an ordinary Linux process given namespaced views of kernel resources, cgroup-enforced limits, a reduced capability and syscall set, and a root filesystem assembled from immutable image layers. Interviewers probe Docker hard because it is the fastest way to find out whether you understand the mechanism or only the commands — the candidate who knows what a layer physically is can explain why `RUN rm secret` still leaks the secret, why exit 137 usually means a cgroup OOM kill rather than a host memory problem, why shell-form CMD breaks graceful shutdown, and why publishing a port walked straight past the host firewall. Each section below builds one mechanism from the kernel upward, then shows where it bites in production; the QA bank and flashcards are the same material compressed into the form these questions actually arrive in.

sections.title: 1. What a Container Actually Is: A Process, Namespaced and Capped
sections.content:
There is no such thing as a container in the Linux kernel. Search the kernel source for a `struct container` and you will not find one. This is the single most important fact in the whole subject, and it is the thing that separates a candidate who has read a blog post from a candidate who has debugged a container at 3am.

What actually happens when you run `docker run nginx` is that a perfectly ordinary Linux process is started — `fork`/`clone` then `execve`, the same as any other program — with three sets of kernel features applied to it:

1. Namespaces change what the process can see. A namespace is a wrapper around a global kernel resource so that processes inside it see their own private instance of it. There is one namespace type per resource: PIDs, mounts, network stack, hostname, IPC objects, user/group IDs, and the cgroup hierarchy. A process in a new PID namespace sees itself as PID 1 and cannot see any other process on the machine, because `/proc` is a view of the PID namespace it is mounted in.
2. Cgroups (control groups) change what the process can use. A cgroup is a node in a kernel-maintained tree that accounts and limits resource consumption for all processes in it: how much memory, how much CPU time, how much block I/O, how many PIDs.
3. A restricted security posture changes what the process can do. Capabilities are dropped, a seccomp filter blocks some syscalls, an LSM (AppArmor or SELinux) profile is applied, and the root filesystem is swapped with `pivot_root` so the process's `/` is your image rather than the host's.

That is the whole trick. There is no boundary object, no hypervisor, no emulation layer. `ps aux` on the host shows the container's processes as normal processes, because they are normal processes.

```
HOST KERNEL  (one kernel, shared by everything)
  |
  +-- PID 4711  nginx: master        <- host's view
  |     namespaces: pid=[4026532...], net=[...], mnt=[...], uts, ipc
  |     cgroup:     /sys/fs/cgroup/system.slice/docker-<id>.scope
  |     rootfs:     /var/lib/docker/overlay2/<id>/merged  (pivot_root'ed)
  |     caps:       14 of ~40 retained,  seccomp: default profile
  |
  |   inside its own PID namespace this same process is PID 1
```

You can prove all of this without Docker. `unshare --pid --fork --mount-proc bash` gives you a shell that thinks it is PID 1. `unshare --net bash` gives you a shell with only a loopback interface. Writing a number into `/sys/fs/cgroup/<group>/memory.max` and then adding a PID to `cgroup.procs` limits that process's memory. Docker's contribution is not the isolation — it is packaging the filesystem (the image) plus the ergonomics, so you do not hand-assemble those primitives yourself.

Interviewers probe this because everything else follows from it. Why is container startup measured in milliseconds? Because there is no kernel to boot — it is just `clone` and `execve`. Why can a container not run a different kernel version, or load a kernel module the host does not have? Because there is only one kernel. Why does a container "see" the host's CPU count in `/proc/cpuinfo` even when you gave it `--cpus=1`? Because `/proc/cpuinfo` is a view of the host kernel's CPU list and there is no "cpu namespace" — the limit lives in a cgroup, in a completely different place, and nothing forces your runtime to look there. Why is a container escape a kernel bug and not a Docker bug? Because the isolation is enforced by kernel code paths that the container's own syscalls reach directly.

The answer to give when asked "what is a container": a process (or process tree) running on the host kernel with namespaced views of kernel resources, cgroup-enforced resource limits, a reduced capability and syscall set, and its own root filesystem assembled from image layers. Then offer to walk any one of those four in detail.
sections.code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Build a "container" by hand, with no container runtime at all.
# Run as root on a Linux host. This is the whole idea in ~20 lines.

set -euo pipefail
ROOT=/tmp/mycontainer
mkdir -p "$ROOT"

# 1. A root filesystem. Steal one from a Docker image (or use debootstrap).
docker export "$(docker create alpine:3.20)" | tar -C "$ROOT" -xf -

# 2. A cgroup with real limits (cgroup v2 unified hierarchy).
CG=/sys/fs/cgroup/handmade
mkdir -p "$CG"
echo "+memory +pids +cpu" > /sys/fs/cgroup/cgroup.subtree_control
echo $((64 * 1024 * 1024)) > "$CG/memory.max"   # 64 MiB hard limit -> OOM kill past this
echo "50000 100000"        > "$CG/cpu.max"      # 50 ms of CPU per 100 ms period = 0.5 CPU
echo 64                    > "$CG/pids.max"     # fork-bomb protection

# 3. A tiny script that the "container" will run as its PID 1.
cat > "$ROOT/inside.sh" <<'INSIDE'
#!/bin/sh
hostname handmade
echo "I am PID $$"          # prints 1
ps -ef                      # only this process tree exists
ip link                     # only lo, and it is DOWN
head -1 /etc/os-release     # Alpine userspace...
uname -r                    # ...running on the HOST kernel
exec /bin/sh
INSIDE
chmod +x "$ROOT/inside.sh"

# 4. Join the cgroup first (children inherit it), then unshare into new namespaces.
#    --mount-proc remounts /proc inside the new PID+mount ns so `ps` sees only us.
#    --root does the pivot_root equivalent so / becomes the extracted image.
echo $$ > "$CG/cgroup.procs"
exec unshare --pid --fork --mount --uts --ipc --net --mount-proc \
             --root="$ROOT" /inside.sh

# What you just built is, minus a security profile and an image format,
# exactly what `docker run --memory=64m --cpus=0.5 --pids-limit=64 alpine sh` does.

sections.title: 2. The Namespaces, One at a Time (and Which Ones Docker Actually Uses)
sections.content:
Linux has eight namespace types. Knowing them by name, and knowing which ones Docker turns on by default, is a very common interview filter because it maps directly to real isolation gaps.

mnt (mount, `CLONE_NEWNS`, 2002) — the oldest one, which is why its constant is named "NEWNS" with no qualifier. It gives the process its own mount table. This is what lets a container have a completely different `/` from the host. The runtime creates the mount namespace, mounts the overlay filesystem, mounts `/proc`, `/sys`, `/dev/pts` and a few tmpfs entries fresh inside it, then calls `pivot_root` to make the image the new root. (`pivot_root`, not `chroot` — `chroot` only changes the path resolution root and is escapable by a process that keeps a file descriptor to a directory outside it; `pivot_root` moves the old root away and it is then unmounted, so there is nothing left to escape to.)

uts (`CLONE_NEWUTS`) — private hostname and domain name. UTS stands for UNIX Time-sharing System, a historical name for the `utsname` struct. This is why `hostname` inside a container returns the container ID and why setting it does not affect the host.

ipc (`CLONE_NEWIPC`) — private System V IPC objects (message queues, semaphores, shared memory segments) and POSIX message queues. Also private `/dev/shm`. This is why two containers cannot see each other's shared-memory segments, and why a database container with a small default `/dev/shm` (64 MB in Docker) breaks PostgreSQL parallel queries or Chrome-based scrapers — `--shm-size=1g` is the fix.

pid (`CLONE_NEWPID`) — private PID number space. The first process in the namespace becomes PID 1 and has the special semantics described later (signal handling and zombie reaping). PID namespaces nest: the host can see and signal container processes by their host PID, but the container cannot see the host's. Note that the PID namespace alone does not hide processes from `ps` — `ps` reads `/proc`, so you also need a fresh `/proc` mounted in a new mount namespace, which is why `unshare --pid` without `--mount-proc` shows you a confusing half-isolated shell.

net (`CLONE_NEWNET`) — a completely separate network stack: its own interfaces, routing table, iptables/nftables rules, socket tables, `/proc/net`. A new net namespace starts with only a down loopback interface. Connectivity is added afterwards by creating a `veth` pair — a virtual cable with two ends — putting one end in the namespace as `eth0` and plugging the other into a bridge on the host.

user (`CLONE_NEWUSER`) — maps UIDs and GIDs, so that UID 0 inside maps to some unprivileged UID outside. Docker does not enable this by default. That is the single biggest thing to know here: by default, root inside a container is root (UID 0) on the host, just with capabilities dropped and a seccomp filter applied. If a kernel bug or a misconfiguration (a mounted Docker socket, `--privileged`, a bind-mounted host path) lets that process out, it is out as root. You opt in with the daemon's `userns-remap` setting, or you use rootless Docker, or in Kubernetes you use user namespaces support (beta in recent versions).

cgroup (`CLONE_NEWCGROUP`, Linux 4.6) — hides the host's cgroup paths, so a process in the container sees its own cgroup as the root of the hierarchy instead of seeing `/sys/fs/cgroup/system.slice/docker-abc123.scope`. Docker enables this with cgroup v2. Without it, `/proc/self/cgroup` leaks the container ID and the host's cgroup layout.

time (`CLONE_NEWTIME`, Linux 5.6) — private offsets for `CLOCK_MONOTONIC` and `CLOCK_BOOTTIME`. Notably it does not virtualise the wall clock (`CLOCK_REALTIME`). Docker does not use it. This is why you cannot give a container a fake current date by any normal means; the system time is the host's.

The practical consequences of what is not namespaced are the interesting part. There is no namespace for the kernel version, so `uname -r` inside an Ubuntu container on an Amazon Linux host reports the host's kernel. There is no namespace for `/proc/cpuinfo`, `/proc/meminfo`, `/proc/loadavg`, or `/sys/devices/system/cpu`, so every runtime that sizes a thread pool from "number of CPUs" or a heap from "total RAM" reads the host's numbers unless it has been specifically taught to read cgroup files. There is no namespace for the system clock, kernel modules, `sysctl` values outside a small namespaced set, or the kernel keyring in the general case.

```
namespace   docker default   what it isolates
---------   --------------   -----------------------------------------
mnt         yes              mount table / the container's /
uts         yes              hostname, NIS domain
ipc         yes              SysV IPC, POSIX mqueues, /dev/shm
pid         yes              process ID space; first proc becomes PID 1
net         yes (except      interfaces, routes, iptables, sockets
            --network=host)
cgroup      yes (v2)         the cgroup path the process can see
user        NO (opt-in)      UID/GID mapping  <-- the big one
time        no               CLOCK_MONOTONIC/BOOTTIME offsets
```

Share namespaces deliberately and you get useful patterns rather than leaks. `--network=container:web` puts a second container in the first one's net namespace — that is exactly how a Kubernetes Pod works internally, with all containers joining the sandbox ("pause") container's net, ipc and uts namespaces so they can reach each other on `localhost`. `--pid=container:web` lets a debug container see and `strace` the target's processes, which is the standard way to debug a distroless image that has no shell of its own.

# Inspect the namespaces of a running container from the host.
CID=$(docker run -d --name web nginx:alpine)
PID=$(docker inspect -f '{{.State.Pid}}' "$CID")

# Every namespace the process is in, as inode numbers. Two processes with the
# same inode for a namespace are in the SAME namespace.
sudo ls -l /proc/$PID/ns/
# lrwxrwxrwx ... cgroup -> 'cgroup:[4026532563]'
# lrwxrwxrwx ... ipc    -> 'ipc:[4026532497]'
# lrwxrwxrwx ... mnt    -> 'mnt:[4026532495]'
# lrwxrwxrwx ... net    -> 'net:[4026532500]'
# lrwxrwxrwx ... pid    -> 'pid:[4026532498]'
# lrwxrwxrwx ... user   -> 'user:[4026531837]'   <-- SAME inode as the host's:
#                                                    no user namespace by default
# lrwxrwxrwx ... uts    -> 'uts:[4026532496]'
sudo readlink /proc/1/ns/user      # compare with host PID 1 -> identical

# lsns gives the whole machine's namespace inventory
sudo lsns -t net -t pid

# Enter just the network namespace of the container using host tools.
# This is the standard trick for debugging networking in an image that
# has no `ip`, `ss`, `tcpdump` or even a shell.
sudo nsenter -t $PID -n ip addr
sudo nsenter -t $PID -n ss -lntp
sudo nsenter -t $PID -n tcpdump -i eth0 -nn -c 20

# Or do it with a container instead of host binaries:
docker run --rm -it --network=container:web --pid=container:web \
  --cap-add=NET_ADMIN --cap-add=SYS_PTRACE nicolaka/netshoot

docker rm -f web

sections.title: 3. Cgroups: How Limits Are Actually Enforced, and Why Your Pod Got OOM-Killed
sections.content:
Namespaces control visibility; cgroups control consumption. They are a completely separate kernel subsystem and they fail in completely different ways, so keep them apart in your head.

A cgroup is a directory in a special filesystem, usually mounted at `/sys/fs/cgroup`. You create a group by making a directory; you add a process by writing its PID into `cgroup.procs`; you set a limit by writing to a controller file. Children inherit and are constrained by their parents. cgroup v2 (the "unified hierarchy", now the default on essentially every modern distro) replaced v1's separate per-controller trees with a single tree where each node enables controllers for its children via `cgroup.subtree_control`. v2 also fixed the biggest accounting hole in v1: page cache and kernel memory are properly attributed to the group that caused them.

Memory. `memory.max` is a hard limit. When a charge would exceed it, the kernel first tries to reclaim pages from that cgroup (dropping clean page cache, swapping if swap is allowed). If reclaim cannot free enough, the cgroup OOM killer runs and kills a process inside that cgroup — not on the host generally. `memory.high` is a softer throttle: crossing it puts the allocating task under heavy reclaim pressure and effectively stalls it, but never kills. `memory.low`/`memory.min` are reclaim protections, not limits. Docker's `--memory` maps to `memory.max`; `--memory-reservation` maps to `memory.low`.

The failure mode you must be able to narrate: your process dies with exit code 137, which is 128 + 9, i.e. SIGKILL. `docker inspect --format '{{.State.OOMKilled}}' <id>` returns `true`, and `dmesg` shows `Memory cgroup out of memory: Killed process ... anon-rss:...`. Note what it does not say: nothing on the host was short of memory. A cgroup OOM kill on a machine with 200 GB free is completely normal — the limit is per-group. Note also the sharp edge: if the killed process happens to be the container's PID 1, the container dies; if it is a worker child, the container keeps running in a degraded state and your health checks may not notice.

The classic root cause is a runtime that does not know about the limit. The JVM historically read `/proc/meminfo` (the host's), computed a default max heap of one quarter of host RAM, and then got killed the moment it grew past the container limit. Modern JVMs (`UseContainerSupport`, on by default since JDK 10 and backported to 8u191) read the cgroup limit and size the heap from `MaxRAMPercentage` instead — but only if the limit is actually set. Node.js still needs `--max-old-space-size` tuned to the limit. Python and Go do not have a heap ceiling at all; Go's answer is `GOMEMLIMIT` (Go 1.19+), a soft target that makes the GC work harder rather than let RSS grow. And remember that RSS is not the only charge: page cache from files your process reads, and tmpfs including `/dev/shm`, are charged to the cgroup too, which is why a container that only reads a big file can be OOM-killed.

CPU. Two different mechanisms, and conflating them is a common interview stumble.

- `cpu.weight` (v2; `cpu.shares` in v1, `--cpu-shares` in Docker) is a relative share used only when the CPU is contended. A group with weight 200 gets twice the runtime of a group with weight 100 when both are runnable. If nothing else wants the CPU, a weight-1 group can use the whole machine. It is a priority, not a cap. (runc converts a v1 share value to a v2 weight with `weight = 1 + ((shares - 2) * 9999) / 262142`, so the familiar default of 1024 shares becomes a weight of 39, not 100.)
- `cpu.max` (v2; `cpu.cfs_quota_us`/`cpu.cfs_period_us` in v1, `--cpus` in Docker) is a hard cap expressed as "quota per period". `--cpus=1.5` writes `150000 100000`: 150 ms of CPU time allowed per 100 ms of wall time. When the group exhausts its quota within a period, every task in it is throttled — descheduled until the next period boundary.

CFS throttling is the single most under-diagnosed latency problem in containerised systems. Imagine a Java service with `--cpus=1` and 40 runnable threads. In the first ~25 ms of a 100 ms period the threads collectively burn the entire 100 ms quota, and then the whole application is frozen for 75 ms. Average CPU utilisation looks like a comfortable 30%, while p99 latency has a 75 ms cliff in it. The evidence is in `cpu.stat`: `nr_throttled` and `throttled_usec` climbing. The fixes are to raise the limit, reduce parallelism to match the limit (`GOMAXPROCS`, JVM `ActiveProcessorCount`, thread pool sizes), or, in Kubernetes, to remove the CPU limit and rely on requests plus weight for isolation — a genuinely contested tradeoff worth having an opinion on.

Other controllers worth naming: `pids.max` (`--pids-limit`) caps the number of tasks and is your fork-bomb defence — a container without it can exhaust the host's PID space and take the node down. `io.max`/`io.weight` for block I/O (only fully effective on the `blk-mq` path with certain filesystems and cgroup v2 writeback). `cpuset.cpus`/`cpuset.mems` pin to specific CPUs and NUMA nodes, which matters for latency-sensitive workloads.

One last thing to say out loud, because it earns credit: CPU is compressible, memory is not. Exceeding a CPU limit slows you down; exceeding a memory limit kills you. That asymmetry is why the standard advice is to set memory requests equal to memory limits and to be far more careful about memory sizing than CPU sizing.
sections.code:
# ---- Reading the truth about a running container's limits (cgroup v2) ----
CID=$(docker run -d --name app --memory=512m --memory-reservation=256m \
        --cpus=1.5 --pids-limit=200 nginx:alpine)

# Docker's own view
docker inspect -f '{{.HostConfig.Memory}} {{.HostConfig.NanoCpus}}' "$CID"

# The kernel's view. Path differs by cgroup driver; systemd driver looks like this:
CG=/sys/fs/cgroup/system.slice/docker-$CID.scope
sudo cat $CG/memory.max      # 536870912
sudo cat $CG/memory.low      # 268435456
sudo cat $CG/cpu.max         # 150000 100000   <- 1.5 CPU
sudo cat $CG/pids.max        # 200
sudo cat $CG/memory.current  # live usage, INCLUDING page cache
sudo cat $CG/memory.stat     # anon / file / slab / sock breakdown

# ---- Is this container being CPU-throttled? The question that solves p99 bugs ----
sudo cat $CG/cpu.stat
# usage_usec 84213000
# nr_periods 41230
# nr_throttled 9871        <- 24% of periods hit the cap
# throttled_usec 512340000 <- 512 seconds of forced stall. This is your latency.

# ---- Reproduce an OOM kill and read the evidence ----
# --shm-size raises the TMPFS size limit so we hit the MEMORY CGROUP, not the
# tmpfs limit. (Docker's default /dev/shm is only 64m, which is itself a common
# source of failures in Postgres and headless-Chrome containers.)
docker run --rm --name oomtest --memory=64m --shm-size=256m alpine sh -c \
  'dd if=/dev/zero of=/dev/shm/fill bs=1M count=200'   # tmpfs pages ARE charged to the cgroup
echo "exit code: $?"                                    # 137 = 128 + SIGKILL(9)
dmesg -T | tail -5                                      # "Memory cgroup out of memory"

# ---- The three settings that stop runtimes guessing from HOST numbers ----
# Go:     GOMAXPROCS to match the CPU cap, GOMEMLIMIT to match the memory cap
docker run -e GOMAXPROCS=2 -e GOMEMLIMIT=450MiB --cpus=2 --memory=512m myapp
# JVM:    let it read the cgroup, then take a percentage of it
docker run --memory=512m eclipse-temurin:21-jre \
  java -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75 -XX:+PrintFlagsFinal -version | grep -i maxheap
# Node:   old space must sit below the container limit, with room for the rest
docker run --memory=512m node:22-alpine node --max-old-space-size=384 app.js

docker rm -f app

sections.title: 4. The Rest of the Sandbox: Capabilities, Seccomp, LSMs, and Rootless
sections.content:
Namespaces and cgroups are about isolation and fairness. Neither of them is a security boundary on its own — a process with full root powers inside a namespace can often reach out of it. The security posture comes from a third layer, and interviewers who care about SRE/platform work will ask about it.

Capabilities. Since Linux 2.2 the powers of root have been split into ~40 distinct capabilities: `CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE` (bind below port 1024), `CAP_NET_ADMIN` (configure interfaces, routes, iptables), `CAP_SYS_ADMIN` (a grab-bag that includes `mount`, and is effectively root), `CAP_SYS_PTRACE`, `CAP_SYS_MODULE` (load kernel modules), `CAP_DAC_OVERRIDE` (bypass file permission checks), and so on. Docker runs containers with a default set of 14 capabilities: CHOWN, DAC_OVERRIDE, FOWNER, FSETID, KILL, SETGID, SETUID, SETPCAP, NET_BIND_SERVICE, NET_RAW, SYS_CHROOT, MKNOD, AUDIT_WRITE, SETFCAP. Everything else — including SYS_ADMIN, SYS_MODULE, SYS_TIME, and NET_ADMIN — is dropped. This is why a container cannot `mount`, cannot change the host clock, and cannot load a module, even as UID 0.

The hardening move is `--cap-drop=ALL` and then add back only what the workload needs, which for most services is nothing at all (if you listen on 8080 rather than 80, you do not even need NET_BIND_SERVICE). The anti-pattern is `--privileged`, which grants all capabilities, disables the seccomp and AppArmor profiles, and exposes all host devices — at that point the only thing left between the container and the host is the mount namespace, and that is trivially crossed.

Seccomp. A BPF filter attached to the process that decides, per syscall number and argument, whether to allow, error, kill, or trace. Docker applies a default profile that blocks roughly 44 of the 300+ syscalls: `kexec_load`, `init_module`, `reboot`, `mount`/`umount2`, `pivot_root`, `bpf`, `perf_event_open`, `add_key`, `keyctl`, `userfaultfd`, `clock_settime`, and others. Much of this profile is deliberately redundant with capabilities — defence in depth, because a capability check bug in one syscall path is then still blocked by the filter. It also occasionally breaks things: older glibc/Docker combinations broke on `clone3` and `faccessat2` until profiles were updated, which is worth knowing as an example of the tradeoff.

LSMs. AppArmor (Debian/Ubuntu) or SELinux (RHEL family) apply a mandatory access control profile. Docker's default AppArmor profile (`docker-default`) denies writes to sensitive `/proc` and `/sys` paths — `/proc/sysrq-trigger`, `/proc/sys/kernel/*`, `/sys/firmware` — that are not otherwise namespaced. SELinux in enforcing mode labels container processes `container_t` and their files `container_file_t`, which is why bind mounts from the host need the `:z` (shared) or `:Z` (private) relabel suffix on RHEL-family hosts or the container gets permission denied on files it apparently owns.

No new privileges. `--security-opt=no-new-privileges` sets the `PR_SET_NO_NEW_PRIVS` process flag, which makes `execve` refuse to grant additional privileges — setuid binaries stop being setuid. This blocks a whole class of escalation from a compromised non-root container process. It is cheap and should be on by default.

User namespaces and rootless. Everything above still leaves UID 0 in the container as UID 0 on the host. A user namespace remaps it: container UID 0 becomes host UID 100000 (say), so even a complete escape lands as an unprivileged user. Docker supports this daemon-wide via `userns-remap`, and rootless Docker goes further by running the daemon itself as a normal user (using `slirp4netns`/`pasta` for networking and `fuse-overlayfs` or native overlay-in-userns for storage). The costs are real: slightly slower networking, no binding to ports below 1024 by default, some storage-driver limitations, and confusing file ownership on bind mounts. Podman is rootless-first, which is much of its appeal.

The things that actually cause escapes in the real world are rarely exotic kernel bugs. They are:
- Mounting the Docker socket (`-v /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock`). Anyone who can talk to that socket can start a new container with `--privileged` and the host root mounted, and is therefore root on the host. Treat socket access as equivalent to giving out the root password. If a CI job or an agent needs to build images, use a rootless builder, or BuildKit's daemonless mode, or a socket proxy that whitelists API endpoints.
- `--privileged`, especially in CI runners and "docker-in-docker" setups.
- Bind-mounting sensitive host paths — `/`, `/etc`, `/var/lib/kubelet`, `/proc`, or a host directory that a host root process later executes from.
- `--pid=host` combined with `CAP_SYS_PTRACE`, which lets you read the memory of host processes.
- Running as root inside the container so that any RCE in your app is immediately UID 0, which makes every one of the above much easier to exploit.

If you want a real security boundary rather than a good isolation boundary, you change the model: gVisor intercepts syscalls in a user-space kernel so the host kernel sees a far smaller surface, or Kata Containers / Firecracker give each container its own lightweight VM and its own kernel. That is the standard answer for multi-tenant untrusted code, and it is why AWS Lambda and Fargate run on Firecracker microVMs rather than on plain containers.

# ---------- A hardened `docker run` for a normal stateless service ----------
#   --user 10001:10001        non-root, NUMERIC so k8s runAsNonRoot can verify it
#   --read-only               immutable rootfs; app cannot rewrite its own binaries
#   --tmpfs /tmp              give back only the scratch space it actually needs
#   --cap-drop=ALL            start from zero capabilities, add back nothing
#   --security-opt=...        PR_SET_NO_NEW_PRIVS: setuid binaries cannot escalate
#   -p 127.0.0.1:8080:8080    bind to loopback, NOT 0.0.0.0 (see the networking section)
docker run -d --name api \
  --user 10001:10001 \
  --read-only \
  --tmpfs /tmp:rw,noexec,nosuid,size=64m \
  --cap-drop=ALL \
  --security-opt=no-new-privileges \
  --pids-limit=200 \
  --memory=512m --cpus=1 \
  -p 127.0.0.1:8080:8080 \
  myorg/api@sha256:9f2c1b0e5d4a3c2b1a0f9e8d7c6b5a49382716253f4e5d6c7b8a9f0e1d2c3b4a5

# The Kubernetes equivalent, which is what you will actually be asked to write:
cat <<'YAML'
securityContext:                 # pod level
  runAsNonRoot: true
  runAsUser: 10001
  fsGroup: 10001
  seccompProfile: { type: RuntimeDefault }
containers:
  - name: api
    securityContext:             # container level
      allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
      readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
      privileged: false
      capabilities: { drop: ["ALL"] }
YAML

# ---------- Prove the capability set is what you think it is ----------
docker run --rm --cap-drop=ALL alpine sh -c 'apk add -q libcap; capsh --print' | grep Current
# Current: =            (empty: no capabilities at all)

docker run --rm alpine sh -c 'apk add -q libcap; capsh --print' | grep Current
# Current: cap_chown,cap_dac_override,...,cap_setfcap=ep   (the default 14)

# ---------- Demonstrate why the docker socket is root ----------
# DO NOT run this anywhere real. It is the standard escape and takes one line.
# docker run --rm -v /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock docker:cli \
#   docker run --rm -v /:/host --privileged alpine chroot /host sh
# => root shell on the HOST. Mounting the socket == handing out host root.

# ---------- Audit an image before you trust it ----------
docker inspect myorg/api:1.4.2 --format '{{.Config.User}}'   # empty string means ROOT
docker run --rm myorg/api:1.4.2 id                            # verify at runtime too

sections.title: 5. Containers Are Not VMs: The Boundary, the Cost, and When to Use Which
sections.content:
"A container is a lightweight VM" is a phrase that will cost you an interview. It is wrong in a way that matters operationally, not just pedantically.

A virtual machine is created by a hypervisor (KVM, Xen, Hyper-V, ESXi) using hardware virtualisation extensions (Intel VT-x, AMD-V). The hypervisor presents virtual hardware — a virtual CPU, a virtual disk controller, a virtual NIC — and the guest boots its own kernel on that hardware. The guest kernel does its own scheduling, its own memory management, its own page tables (accelerated by nested paging: EPT/NPT). The interface between guest and host is the hardware interface plus a small set of paravirtualised device channels (virtio). When guest code executes a privileged instruction or touches an emulated device, it causes a VM exit into the hypervisor.

A container is a process on the host kernel. There is no guest kernel, no virtual hardware, no VM exit. When your containerised app calls `read()`, that syscall lands in the host kernel, in exactly the same code path as a syscall from a process you started from your own shell.

That difference produces every practical consequence:

```
                        VIRTUAL MACHINE            CONTAINER
kernel                  its own guest kernel       shares the host kernel
startup                 firmware+kernel+init:      clone() + execve():
                        seconds                    milliseconds
baseline memory         hundreds of MB of guest    only what your process uses
disk image              GBs, opaque                layers, shared + deduplicated
density per host        tens                       hundreds to thousands
isolation surface       hypervisor + virtio        the entire syscall ABI
                        (small, heavily audited)   (300+ calls into 30M lines of C)
different OS or kernel  yes                        no
live migration          yes                        no
```

Isolation strength is the real distinction. A container escape needs a bug in the kernel's handling of a syscall — and the kernel is a ~30-million-line C program that the attacker can call into 300+ different ways with arbitrary arguments. A VM escape needs a bug in the hypervisor's much smaller and much more paranoid interface. Both happen; the base rates are very different. This is why the honest formulation is: containers isolate workloads you trust from each other's bugs and resource appetites; VMs isolate workloads you do not trust. If you are running arbitrary customer-supplied code, you use VMs or something VM-backed.

Kernel sharing has non-security consequences too, and mentioning them shows operational depth:
- A container image is not portable across kernels — a Linux container cannot run on a Windows kernel and vice versa. Docker Desktop on macOS and Windows is not running containers natively; it runs a Linux VM (LinuxKit on the Hyper-V/Virtualization.framework) and your containers are processes inside that. This is why file I/O on macOS bind mounts is slow: it crosses a VM boundary through virtiofs.
- Kernel settings are largely shared. Many `sysctl`s are not namespaced; if one container needs `vm.max_map_count` raised (Elasticsearch famously does), you raise it on the host and every container gets it.
- A kernel panic or a host-level OOM takes down every container on the node. A VM's guest panic takes down only that VM.
- Kernel upgrades require draining the node, because every container on it shares the kernel being replaced.
- Anything that needs a kernel module (some VPNs, some storage drivers, eBPF-heavy tooling) needs it loaded on the host, not in the image.

The hybrid answers are the most interesting part of this question and are what a senior candidate reaches for. gVisor (Google) runs a user-space kernel called Sentry that implements most of the Linux syscall ABI itself; the container's syscalls are intercepted (via KVM or ptrace) and handled in user space, so the host kernel sees only a tiny, restricted syscall set from the Sentry process. It costs some syscall-heavy performance and does not implement 100% of Linux. Kata Containers gives each pod a lightweight VM with its own kernel while still speaking the container/OCI and CRI interfaces, so it drops into Kubernetes as a RuntimeClass. Firecracker (AWS) is a minimal VMM written in Rust with a deliberately tiny device model, booting a microVM in ~125 ms with a few MB of overhead; it is the substrate under Lambda and Fargate, and it exists precisely because AWS needed VM-grade isolation at container-grade density and startup.

So the answer to "when would you use a VM instead of a container" is: when you need a different kernel or OS, when you need kernel-module-level control, when the workload is untrusted or subject to hard multi-tenant compliance boundaries, or when you need live migration. And the good closing line is that in practice it is not either/or — nearly every container in production today is already running inside a VM, because that is what an EC2 instance or a GCE node is.

---

kind: Pod
metadata: { name: untrusted-job }
spec:
  runtimeClassName: gvisor      # same YAML, VM-ish isolation, no app changes

YAML

sections.title: 6. Images vs Containers: Layers, OverlayFS, Copy-Up, and Whiteouts
sections.content:
An image is a read-only template: an ordered list of filesystem layers plus a configuration blob that says how to start a process from them. A container is a running (or stopped) instance of that template with one extra, thin, writable layer on top. The relationship is exactly class-to-object, or executable-to-process — one image, many containers, all sharing the same immutable layers on disk.

Concretely, an OCI image on a registry is three kinds of object, all content-addressed by SHA-256 digest:

1. Layer blobs — gzip- (or zstd-) compressed tar archives, each one a diff: the set of files added, changed, or deleted relative to the layer below.
2. A config blob — JSON containing the default `Env`, `Cmd`, `Entrypoint`, `User`, `WorkingDir`, `ExposedPorts`, `Labels`, plus `rootfs.diff_ids` (the digests of the uncompressed layer tars, in order) and a `history` array.
3. A manifest — JSON listing the config digest and the layer digests with their media types and sizes.

Two digests get confused constantly, and being precise here reads well. The image ID you see in `docker images` is the SHA-256 of the config blob. The repo digest (`myimage@sha256:...`, what you pin in production) is the SHA-256 of the manifest. They are different values for the same image. And the layer digests in the manifest are digests of the compressed blobs, while `diff_ids` in the config are digests of the uncompressed tars — which is why the same logical layer can have two different hashes depending on which one you are looking at.

How the layers become one filesystem. Docker's default storage driver on Linux is `overlay2`, backed by the kernel's OverlayFS. OverlayFS takes a stack of read-only directories (`lowerdir`, listed top-first), one writable directory (`upperdir`), a `workdir` for atomic operations, and presents a unified view at `merged`. Lookups walk the stack top-down and return the first hit.

```
merged/  (what the container sees as /)
  ^
  |  upperdir   -> /var/lib/docker/overlay2/<container>/diff   [READ-WRITE, per container]
  |  lowerdir-0 -> layer from `COPY . /app`                    [read-only, shared]
  |  lowerdir-1 -> layer from `RUN pip install -r req.txt`     [read-only, shared]
  |  lowerdir-2 -> layer from the base image python:3.12-slim  [read-only, shared]
```

Three behaviours fall out of this and each is a production issue:

Copy-up. The first time a container writes to a file that lives in a lower layer, OverlayFS copies the entire file up to the writable layer before applying the change. Appending one byte to a 2 GB log file that shipped in the image costs a 2 GB copy and 2 GB of extra disk, and the container stalls while it happens. This is why databases and anything write-heavy must write to a volume, not to the container's writable layer, and why "the container is slow on first write" is a real diagnosis.

Whiteouts. Deleting a file that exists in a lower layer cannot actually remove it — lower layers are immutable and shared. Instead OverlayFS creates a whiteout: a character device with major/minor 0/0 in the upper layer that masks the name below. In the OCI tar layer format the same idea is encoded as a zero-length file named `.wh.<name>` (and `.wh..wh..opq` to mark a whole directory opaque). The consequence is the single most common image mistake:

```dockerfile
COPY secrets.json /app/           # layer 4: file is now in a blob, forever
RUN rm /app/secrets.json          # layer 5: adds a whiteout. Image is BIGGER.
```
The secret is still in layer 4. Anyone who pulls the image can extract it with `docker save` and `tar`. Deleting in a later layer hides a file from the running container; it never removes it from the image. The only fixes are: never add it (use a BuildKit secret mount), or discard the layer entirely with a multi-stage build.

Sharing. Because layers are content-addressed and read-only, twenty containers from the same image share exactly one copy on disk and, for the executable pages they map, one copy in the page cache. This is most of why container density is so much higher than VM density, and it is the reason to standardise on a common base image across your fleet: your nodes then pull and cache one base layer instead of eight.

Note the storage-driver family, because it comes up on non-Linux and older systems: `overlay2` (the default, kernel OverlayFS), `btrfs`/`zfs` (snapshot-based, use the filesystem's own CoW), `devicemapper` (block-level CoW, legacy and removed in recent Docker), `fuse-overlayfs` (for rootless where the kernel cannot mount overlay in a user namespace on older kernels), and `vfs` (no CoW at all — a full copy per layer; correct everywhere, hopelessly inefficient, used as a fallback and in some nested-container CI setups).

# The manifest lists the config + layers

# The config blob holds Env/Cmd/Entrypoint AND rootfs.diff_ids

  --format 'imageID(config)={{.Id}}{{"\n"}}repoDigest(manifest)={{index .RepoDigests 0}}'

# ---------- Where the merged filesystem physically lives ----------
CID=$(docker run -d --name demo alpine sleep 300)
sudo docker inspect "$CID" --format '{{json .GraphDriver.Data}}' | jq .
# { "LowerDir": "/var/lib/docker/overlay2/xxx/diff:...",
#   "MergedDir": "/var/lib/docker/overlay2/yyy/merged",
#   "UpperDir":  "/var/lib/docker/overlay2/yyy/diff",     <- the writable layer
#   "WorkDir":   "/var/lib/docker/overlay2/yyy/work" }

# ---------- See copy-up and whiteouts happen ----------
docker exec demo sh -c 'echo hello > /newfile; rm /etc/hostname; sed -i "1i x" /etc/hosts'
docker diff demo
#  A /newfile          <- Added
#  C /etc              <- Changed (dir)
#  D /etc/hostname     <- Deleted -> a whiteout in the upper layer
#  C /etc/hosts        <- Changed -> the WHOLE file was copied up first
UPPER=$(sudo docker inspect demo --format '{{.GraphDriver.Data.UpperDir}}')
sudo ls -la "$UPPER/etc/"
# c--------- 1 root root 0, 0 ... hostname   <- char device 0/0 = the whiteout marker

printf 'AWS_SECRET=hunter2\n' > /tmp/secrets.env
cat > /tmp/Dockerfile.leak <<'EOF'

COPY secrets.env /secrets.env
RUN rm -f /secrets.env          # "deleted"
EOF
docker build -f /tmp/Dockerfile.leak -t leaky /tmp
docker run --rm leaky ls /secrets.env        # No such file — looks safe...
docker save leaky | tar -xO --wildcards '*/layer.tar' 2>/dev/null | strings | grep hunter2
# hunter2   <- still sitting in a layer blob. The image leaks the secret.

docker rm -f demo

sections.title: 7. Layer Caching: Why Your Build Takes 9 Minutes and How to Make It 20 Seconds
sections.content:
Every instruction in a Dockerfile that changes the filesystem produces a layer, and the builder caches those layers. Understanding the exact cache-hit rule is the difference between a build that reinstalls your entire dependency tree on every commit and one that does not.

The rule, for the classic builder and for BuildKit alike: for each instruction, the builder computes a cache key from the parent layer's identity plus the instruction itself, and for `COPY`/`ADD` plus a checksum of the file contents being copied (content, size, mode, ownership — but not mtime). If a cached layer with that key exists, it is reused and the instruction is not executed. If not, the instruction runs and, crucially, every subsequent instruction is a guaranteed miss, because their parent identity has now changed. Cache invalidation cascades downward and never recovers.

For `RUN`, only the command string is part of the key. The builder has no idea what the command does. `RUN apt-get update` will hit the cache forever, serving you a package index from three months ago, and then `RUN apt-get install -y curl` in a later layer tries to fetch a `.deb` version that no longer exists on the mirror and fails with a 404. This is the canonical "cache staleness" bug and it is why the two commands must be in a single `RUN`:

```dockerfile
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends curl ca-certificates \
    && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*
```
The `rm` must be in the same `RUN` too. In a separate `RUN` it only adds a whiteout while the ~40 MB of package lists stay in the earlier layer.

The one optimisation that matters most is ordering instructions from least-frequently-changing to most-frequently-changing, and separating dependency manifests from source code. Almost every slow build in the wild is this mistake:

```dockerfile
COPY . .                       # any source change invalidates here...
RUN npm ci                     # ...so this re-runs every single build
```
versus:
```dockerfile
COPY package.json package-lock.json ./
RUN npm ci                     # only re-runs when the lockfile actually changes
COPY . .                       # source churn invalidates only this cheap layer
```
The same shape applies everywhere: `go.mod`/`go.sum` then `go mod download`; `requirements.txt` or `poetry.lock` then `pip install`; `pom.xml` then `mvn dependency:go-offline`; `Cargo.toml` then a dummy build to warm the dependency cache.

`.dockerignore` is not cosmetic. The build context is everything under the build directory, and with the classic builder it is tarred and shipped to the daemon before the build even starts. Without a `.dockerignore`, `COPY . .` sends and copies `.git` (often hundreds of MB), `node_modules` (which then shadows the ones you carefully installed, frequently with binaries built for the wrong platform), build output, `.env` files with real credentials, and CI caches. It bloats the image, leaks secrets, and — because those directories change constantly — destroys the cache hit on your `COPY` layer.

BuildKit changes the picture substantially and is the default builder in modern Docker. It parses the Dockerfile into a DAG rather than a linear script, so independent stages build in parallel and stages nothing depends on are skipped entirely. It transfers only the files a `COPY` actually needs, incrementally. And it adds mount types that solve caching problems the old model could not:

- `RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.m2` gives you a directory that persists between builds but is never committed into a layer. This is the correct home for package-manager caches — Go's build cache, `~/.cache/pip`, `~/.m2`, `~/.npm`, `/var/cache/apt`. It gives you warm dependency downloads even when the lockfile changed, and zero image size cost.
- `RUN --mount=type=secret,id=token` exposes a secret as a file for the duration of one command, never in any layer, never in `docker history`.
- `RUN --mount=type=bind,from=stage,source=/x,target=/x` reads from another stage without copying it in.
- `COPY --link` creates the copied layer independently of the parent chain, so changing the base image does not force the copy to redo — a large win for images built on a frequently-patched base.

Cache across machines. Your laptop's cache is local to the builder; a fresh CI runner has none, which is why CI builds are slow even when the Dockerfile is perfect. The fix is an exported cache: `--cache-to type=registry,ref=myrepo/app:buildcache,mode=max` and `--cache-from type=registry,ref=myrepo/app:buildcache`. `mode=max` exports intermediate layers too, not just the final ones, which is what makes multi-stage builds cacheable. GitHub Actions has `type=gha`; there is also `type=local`, `type=s3`, and `type=inline` (cheap, embeds cache metadata in the image itself, but only covers the final stage).

Finally, know how to look at the cache instead of guessing. `docker build --progress=plain` prints `CACHED` next to every reused step, so you can see exactly where the chain broke, and `docker history --no-trunc` shows the per-layer size that tells you which instruction is making the image fat.

# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1
# ============================================================================
# A Node service. Same app, correct layering, BuildKit cache mounts.
# Cold build ~90s; warm build after a source-only change ~4s.
# ============================================================================
FROM node:22-bookworm-slim AS deps
WORKDIR /app

# 1. ONLY the dependency manifests. This layer's cache key depends on the
#    lockfile contents alone, so 99% of commits hit it.
COPY package.json package-lock.json ./

# 2. A cache mount: ~/.npm survives between builds but is NOT in the image.
#    Even when the lockfile DOES change, the tarballs are already local.
#    sharing=locked prevents two concurrent builds corrupting the cache dir.
RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.npm,sharing=locked \
    npm ci --omit=dev

# 3. A private registry token that must never reach a layer or `docker history`.
#    Build with:  docker build --secret id=npmrc,src=$HOME/.npmrc .
# RUN --mount=type=secret,id=npmrc,target=/root/.npmrc npm ci --omit=dev

FROM node:22-bookworm-slim AS runtime
ENV NODE_ENV=production
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=deps /app/node_modules ./node_modules
# 4. Source LAST, because it changes on every commit. Only this cheap layer
#    and anything after it is rebuilt.
COPY --chown=node:node . .
USER node
EXPOSE 8080
CMD ["node", "server.js"]

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# .dockerignore  — write this BEFORE the Dockerfile, every time.
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# .git
# .gitignore
# node_modules
# npm-debug.log
# dist
# coverage
# .env
# .env.*
# **/*.md
# .github
# Dockerfile*
# docker-compose*.yml

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Debian/Ubuntu: the one-RUN rule, and why each piece is there
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# RUN apt-get update \
#  && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends \
#        ca-certificates curl \
#  && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*
#
#  same RUN as update ....... or the cached index goes stale and installs 404
#  --no-install-recommends .. skips "suggested" packages; often halves the size
#  rm -rf .../lists ......... same RUN, or the ~40MB stays in the earlier layer

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Seeing and sharing the cache
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Where did the cache break?  Look for "CACHED" per step.
docker build --progress=plain -t app:dev . 2>&1 | grep -E '^#[0-9]+ (CACHED|\[)'

# Which instruction made the image fat?
docker history --no-trunc --format '{{.Size}}\t{{.CreatedBy}}' app:dev | head -20

# Persist the cache across ephemeral CI runners (mode=max = intermediate stages too)
docker buildx build \
  --cache-from type=registry,ref=ghcr.io/org/app:buildcache \
  --cache-to   type=registry,ref=ghcr.io/org/app:buildcache,mode=max \
  --tag ghcr.io/org/app:$GIT_SHA --push .

sections.title: 8. Dockerfile Instructions: Precise Semantics and the Best Practice Behind Each
sections.content:
Most Dockerfile advice is repeated without the reason attached. Here is each instruction that matters, what it actually does, and the failure it prevents.

`FROM` starts a stage and sets the base. Three levels of pinning: `FROM node` (terrible — `latest` is a moving target and your build is not reproducible), `FROM node:22-bookworm-slim` (acceptable — a tag that still moves for patches), `FROM node:22-bookworm-slim@sha256:...` (reproducible — the digest is immutable). Digest pinning plus an automated bumper (Renovate, Dependabot) is the production answer: you get byte-identical rebuilds and you still get security patches, but as a reviewable pull request rather than a silent change. `FROM x AS name` names a stage; `FROM scratch` starts from nothing.

`RUN` executes in a new layer. Two forms. Shell form `RUN apt-get update` becomes `/bin/sh -c "apt-get update"`, so shell features — pipes, `&&`, variable expansion, globs — work. Exec form `RUN ["apt-get", "update"]` executes directly with no shell, so none of those work. For `RUN` the shell form is usually what you want. Note that `sh -c` returns the exit code of the last command in a pipeline by default, so `RUN curl -f url | tar xz` silently succeeds if `curl` fails — put `SHELL ["/bin/bash", "-o", "pipefail", "-c"]` near the top of the Dockerfile if you use pipes.

`COPY` vs `ADD`. Use `COPY`. `ADD` has two surprising behaviours: it auto-extracts local tar archives into the destination, and it can fetch remote URLs (which it does not extract). Both make the Dockerfile's effect non-obvious to a reader, and the URL fetch historically had no integrity check, so you were installing whatever was at that URL today. The only good reasons to use `ADD` are the deliberate tar extraction and, with a recent BuildKit frontend, `ADD --checksum=sha256:...` for a verified remote fetch. `COPY --from=stage` and `COPY --from=image` pull from another stage or a published image. `COPY --chown=user:group` sets ownership at copy time, which avoids a whole extra `RUN chown -R` layer that would duplicate every file it touches. `COPY --chmod=` sets the mode. `COPY --link` makes the resulting layer independent of the parent chain so base-image changes do not invalidate it.

`WORKDIR` sets the working directory for everything after it, and creates it if missing. Use it rather than `RUN cd /app` — a `cd` inside a `RUN` affects only that one shell and is gone by the next instruction, which is a classic confusion.

`ENV` vs `ARG`. `ARG` is a build-time variable: available to instructions during the build, settable with `--build-arg`, and not present in the final image's environment. `ENV` is baked into the image config and is present in every container started from it, and it also overrides an `ARG` of the same name. Critically, neither is a secret: `ARG` values appear in `docker history` and in the image's build metadata, and `ENV` values are visible in `docker inspect` to anyone who can pull the image. An `ARG NPM_TOKEN` passed with `--build-arg` is a leak. Use `RUN --mount=type=secret` instead. An `ARG` declared before the first `FROM` is global and must be re-declared inside a stage to be used there.

`USER`. The default is root, which means any RCE in your application is root inside the container and, without user namespaces, UID 0 on the host. Create a user in the image and switch to it. Prefer a numeric UID (`USER 10001`) over a name: Kubernetes' `runAsNonRoot: true` check reads the image config and cannot verify that a name is non-root, so a name-only `USER` fails the admission check. Also remember that switching to non-root means the process can no longer bind ports below 1024 — listen on 8080 and map it, do not reach for `CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE`.

`EXPOSE` publishes nothing. It is documentation in the image metadata that `docker run -P` and some tooling read. Ports reach the outside world only via `-p`/`--publish` or a Compose/Kubernetes port mapping.

`HEALTHCHECK` defines a command the daemon runs periodically inside the container; exit 0 means healthy, exit 1 means unhealthy. Options: `--interval`, `--timeout`, `--retries`, `--start-period` (a grace window during which failures do not count against the retry budget — essential for slow-starting JVM apps). Docker marks the container `healthy`/`unhealthy` but does not restart it on its own; Swarm and Compose's `depends_on: condition: service_healthy` act on it, and Kubernetes ignores it entirely in favour of its own probes. Write the check against your app's actual readiness (can it reach its database?), not just "is the port open".

`STOPSIGNAL` changes the signal sent on `docker stop` from SIGTERM. Useful for images whose PID 1 expects something else — nginx wants SIGQUIT for a graceful drain, and `STOPSIGNAL SIGQUIT` gets you that.

`LABEL` attaches metadata. Use the OCI standard keys (`org.opencontainers.image.source`, `.revision`, `.created`, `.licenses`) — `image.source` pointing at your Git repo is what makes GitHub link a package to its repository, and `.revision` with the commit SHA is what turns "which build is this?" into a one-command answer months later.

`VOLUME` is almost always a mistake in an application Dockerfile. It declares a path as an anonymous volume mount point, which means (a) every `docker run` silently creates a new unnamed volume that nobody ever cleans up, and (b) any `RUN` after the `VOLUME` that writes to that path has its changes discarded, because the write goes into the temporary volume rather than the layer. Let the operator decide mounts at run time.

`SHELL` changes the shell used by shell-form `RUN`. Two real uses: enabling `pipefail` on Linux, and switching to PowerShell on Windows images.

`ONBUILD` registers an instruction that fires when the image is used as a base. It surprises people badly (a build does things not written in its own Dockerfile) and multi-stage builds have made it largely obsolete.

# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1
# =============================================================================
# A reference Python service Dockerfile with the reasoning inline.
# =============================================================================

# Digest pin: reproducible builds. Renovate/Dependabot bumps it as a reviewable PR.
# Get the real value with:  docker buildx imagetools inspect python:3.12-slim-bookworm
FROM python:3.12-slim-bookworm@sha256:PUT_THE_REAL_DIGEST_HERE AS base

# pipefail: without this, `RUN curl -f url | sh` succeeds even when curl 404s.
SHELL ["/bin/bash", "-o", "pipefail", "-c"]

ENV PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1 \
    PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1 \
    PIP_NO_CACHE_DIR=1 \
    PIP_DISABLE_PIP_VERSION_CHECK=1

# ---- build stage: compilers live here and never reach the runtime image ----
FROM base AS build
RUN apt-get update \
 && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends build-essential libpq-dev \
 && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*
WORKDIR /app
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.cache/pip \
    pip install --prefix=/install -r requirements.txt

# ---- runtime stage ----
FROM base AS runtime
RUN apt-get update \
 && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends libpq5 \
 && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/* \
 && groupadd --gid 10001 app \
 && useradd  --uid 10001 --gid app --no-create-home --shell /usr/sbin/nologin app

COPY --from=build /install /usr/local
WORKDIR /app
COPY --chown=10001:10001 . .

# NUMERIC uid: k8s `runAsNonRoot: true` cannot verify a username.
USER 10001

# Documentation only. It publishes nothing.
EXPOSE 8080

# start-period gives a slow boot room before failures count.
HEALTHCHECK --interval=30s --timeout=3s --start-period=20s --retries=3 \
  CMD python -c "import urllib.request,sys; sys.exit(0 if urllib.request.urlopen('http://127.0.0.1:8080/healthz', timeout=2).status==200 else 1)"

# OCI labels: this is what makes a mystery image traceable six months later.
ARG GIT_SHA=unknown
LABEL org.opencontainers.image.source="https://github.com/org/repo" \
      org.opencontainers.image.revision="${GIT_SHA}" \
      org.opencontainers.image.licenses="Apache-2.0"

ENTRYPOINT ["gunicorn"]
CMD ["--bind", "0.0.0.0:8080", "--workers", "4", "app:application"]

# =============================================================================
# WHAT NOT TO DO — every line here is a real bug
# =============================================================================
# FROM python                      # `latest`: not reproducible, changes silently
# ADD https://example.com/x.tgz /  # unverified remote fetch, does not extract
# ARG DB_PASSWORD                  # visible in `docker history` FOREVER
# ENV AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY=...    # visible in `docker inspect` to anyone
# RUN cd /app && make              # the cd evaporates; use WORKDIR
# COPY . .                         # before the deps layer: destroys all caching
# RUN pip install -r req.txt       # ...so this reruns on every source edit
# VOLUME /app/data                 # anonymous volume per run + later RUNs discarded
# RUN chmod -R 777 /app            # duplicates every file into a new layer
# USER appuser                     # non-numeric: fails k8s runAsNonRoot
# (no USER at all)                 # container runs as root == host uid 0

# Verify the anti-patterns are absent:
#   docker history --no-trunc myimage | grep -iE 'password|token|secret|key'
#   docker inspect myimage --format '{{json .Config.Env}}'
#   docker inspect myimage --format 'user={{.Config.User}}'

sections.title: 9. ENTRYPOINT vs CMD, Shell vs Exec Form, and the PID 1 Problem
sections.content:
This is the highest-frequency Docker interview question that candidates get half-right, because the two-by-two of (ENTRYPOINT, CMD) x (shell form, exec form) has a genuinely non-obvious interaction, and because the PID 1 consequences only show up in production.

The combination rule. At container start, the command executed is `ENTRYPOINT` with `CMD` appended as arguments.

- `ENTRYPOINT ["ping"]` + `CMD ["-c", "3", "localhost"]` runs `ping -c 3 localhost`.
- `docker run img example.com` replaces CMD only, giving `ping example.com`. CMD is the default arguments, easy to override.
- `docker run --entrypoint=sh img` replaces the entrypoint. Note the sharp edge: `--entrypoint` takes only the executable; any arguments go after the image name.
- With no ENTRYPOINT, `CMD` is the whole command.
- With an ENTRYPOINT in exec form and a `CMD` in shell form, the CMD becomes the three arguments `/bin/sh -c "<cmd>"` appended to the entrypoint — almost never what anyone wants.
- Setting `ENTRYPOINT` in a Dockerfile resets any inherited `CMD` to empty, so if you set ENTRYPOINT you must set CMD again.

Choosing between them. Use `ENTRYPOINT` when the image is a program and you want `docker run myimage --flag` to feel like running that program (`ENTRYPOINT ["nginx"]`, `ENTRYPOINT ["/usr/bin/myserver"]`). Use `CMD` alone when the image is an environment and you want `docker run myimage bash` to work naturally. The common production pattern is `ENTRYPOINT ["/entrypoint.sh"]` for a small script that does setup (wait for a dependency, render a config from environment variables, drop privileges) and then `exec "$@"` — the `exec` is essential, because it replaces the shell with your process so your process becomes PID 1 rather than a child of a shell that will not forward signals.

Shell form is where the real bug lives. `CMD python app.py` is rewritten to `CMD ["/bin/sh", "-c", "python app.py"]`. Now `/bin/sh` is PID 1, and your Python process is its child. When `docker stop` fires, SIGTERM goes to PID 1 — the shell — which has no handler for it and does not forward it. Your application never learns it should shut down. Ten seconds later Docker escalates to SIGKILL, the container dies with exit code 137, in-flight requests are dropped, and the database connection pool is never closed. (Some shells optimise a single simple command in `sh -c` into an `exec`, which accidentally saves you; the moment your command has a `&&`, a pipe, a redirect, or a variable expansion, the shell stays resident and the bug is real. Do not rely on the optimisation.) Shell form also blocks argument overriding: `docker run img extra-arg` appends `extra-arg` as an argument to `/bin/sh`, not to your program.

So: exec form (`["cmd", "arg"]`) for ENTRYPOINT and CMD, always, and if you genuinely need shell features — variable expansion in the command line, for example — be explicit about it: `ENTRYPOINT ["/bin/sh", "-c", "exec myapp --port ${PORT}"]`, with the `exec` written by hand.

The PID 1 problem is a separate and deeper issue. In a PID namespace, the first process gets special kernel treatment (`man 7 pid_namespaces`):

1. Default signal dispositions do not apply. For any signal other than SIGKILL and SIGSTOP, if PID 1 has not installed a handler, the signal is discarded. Normally SIGTERM's default action kills a process; for PID 1 it does nothing. So a program that never installed a SIGTERM handler — which is most shells, and many simple scripts — is literally immune to `docker stop`, and always takes the full grace period followed by SIGKILL.
2. PID 1 must reap zombies. When a process's parent dies, the orphan is reparented to PID 1 of its namespace. If PID 1 never calls `wait()`, every such orphan stays as a zombie holding a PID slot. An app that shells out frequently and does not reap accumulates thousands of `<defunct>` entries and eventually hits `pids.max` or the host's PID limit, at which point `fork()` starts failing everywhere.
3. If PID 1 exits, the whole namespace is torn down — every other process in the container is killed.

The fix is a tiny init: `docker run --init` inserts `tini` as PID 1, which forwards signals to your process and reaps orphans; in Kubernetes you set `shareProcessNamespace` or bake `tini`/`dumb-init` into the image as the entrypoint (`ENTRYPOINT ["/sbin/tini", "--", "myapp"]`). You need it whenever your PID 1 is a shell script, a language runtime that spawns child processes, or anything that does not handle signals itself.

Graceful shutdown, end to end, is the thing this all exists to enable: `docker stop` sends `STOPSIGNAL` (default SIGTERM) to PID 1, waits `--time` seconds (default 10), then SIGKILL. Your process should catch SIGTERM, stop accepting new work, fail its readiness probe so the load balancer stops routing to it, finish in-flight requests, close connections, and exit 0. In Kubernetes the same contract is `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` (default 30) and a `preStop` hook, with the endpoint removal racing the SIGTERM — which is why a `preStop: sleep 5` is such a common workaround.

# =============================================================================
# The four combinations, with the exact command each produces
# =============================================================================
# Dockerfile A:  CMD ["echo", "hello"]
#   docker run img            -> echo hello
#   docker run img echo bye   -> echo bye              (CMD fully replaced)
#
# Dockerfile B:  ENTRYPOINT ["echo"]
#   docker run img            -> echo
#   docker run img hello      -> echo hello            (args APPENDED)
#
# Dockerfile C:  ENTRYPOINT ["ping"]  +  CMD ["-c","3","localhost"]
#   docker run img            -> ping -c 3 localhost
#   docker run img 8.8.8.8    -> ping 8.8.8.8          (only CMD replaced)
#   docker run --entrypoint=sh img -c 'echo hi'  -> sh -c 'echo hi'
#
# Dockerfile D:  CMD echo hello        (SHELL form)
#   docker run img            -> /bin/sh -c "echo hello"
#   PID 1 is /bin/sh. SIGTERM goes to the shell, not to echo.

# =============================================================================
# Prove the signal bug, then prove the fix
# =============================================================================
cat > /tmp/app.py <<'PY'
import signal, sys, time
def bye(signum, frame):
    print(f"caught {signal.Signals(signum).name} - draining", flush=True)
    time.sleep(1); print("clean exit", flush=True); sys.exit(0)
signal.signal(signal.SIGTERM, bye)
print("serving as pid", __import__("os").getpid(), flush=True)
while True: time.sleep(1)
PY

# --- BROKEN: shell form + a compound command, so sh stays as PID 1 ---
cat > /tmp/Dockerfile.bad <<'EOF'
FROM python:3.12-slim
COPY app.py /app.py
CMD echo starting && python /app.py
EOF
docker build -q -f /tmp/Dockerfile.bad -t sig-bad /tmp
docker run -d --name bad sig-bad >/dev/null
docker exec bad cat /proc/1/comm     # "sh"  <- PID 1 is the shell, not python
docker top bad                       # from the HOST, so it works even with no `ps` in the image
time docker stop bad                 # takes the full 10s, and logs no "caught SIGTERM"
docker inspect bad --format 'exit={{.State.ExitCode}}'   # exit=137 (SIGKILL)

# --- FIXED: exec form, so python IS PID 1 and receives the signal ---
cat > /tmp/Dockerfile.good <<'EOF'
FROM python:3.12-slim
COPY app.py /app.py
CMD ["python", "/app.py"]
EOF
docker build -q -f /tmp/Dockerfile.good -t sig-good /tmp
docker run -d --name good sig-good >/dev/null
time docker stop good                # ~1s
docker logs good                     # "caught SIGTERM - draining" / "clean exit"
docker inspect good --format 'exit={{.State.ExitCode}}'  # exit=0
docker rm -f bad good

# =============================================================================
# The entrypoint-script pattern. The `exec` on the last line is the whole point.
# =============================================================================
cat <<'SH'
#!/bin/sh
set -e

# 1. render config from env
envsubst < /etc/app/config.tmpl > /etc/app/config.yaml

# 2. wait for a dependency (Compose depends_on does not guarantee readiness)
until nc -z "${DB_HOST:-db}" 5432; do echo "waiting for db"; sleep 1; done

# 3. hand over. `exec` REPLACES this shell, so the app becomes PID 1 and
#    receives SIGTERM directly. Without `exec`, the shell stays as PID 1
#    and your app never sees the shutdown signal.
exec "$@"
SH
# Dockerfile:
#   COPY entrypoint.sh /entrypoint.sh
#   ENTRYPOINT ["/entrypoint.sh"]
#   CMD ["gunicorn", "--bind", "0.0.0.0:8080", "app:application"]

# =============================================================================
# When you cannot make your app PID 1 well-behaved: use an init
# =============================================================================
docker run --init myimage             # docker injects tini as PID 1
# or bake it in:
#   RUN apt-get install -y tini
#   ENTRYPOINT ["/usr/bin/tini", "--", "/entrypoint.sh"]
# nginx wants SIGQUIT for a graceful drain, not SIGTERM:
#   STOPSIGNAL SIGQUIT

sections.title: 10. Multi-Stage Builds: Small Images, No Toolchain, No Leaked Secrets
sections.content:
Before multi-stage builds existed, teams maintained two Dockerfiles — one "builder" image with the compiler and one "runtime" image — plus a shell script that ran the first, copied artefacts out with `docker cp`, and fed them into the second. Multi-stage builds collapse all of that into one file: multiple `FROM` instructions, each starting a fresh stage, with `COPY --from=` to pull artefacts across the boundary.

```dockerfile
FROM golang:1.23 AS build          # stage 0: ~850 MB, has the whole toolchain
WORKDIR /src
COPY go.mod go.sum ./
RUN go mod download
COPY . .
RUN CGO_ENABLED=0 go build -o /out/server ./cmd/server

FROM gcr.io/distroless/static:nonroot   # stage 1: ~2 MB
COPY --from=build /out/server /server
USER nonroot:nonroot
ENTRYPOINT ["/server"]
```
The final image contains only the layers of the last stage. Everything in stage 0 — Go, gcc, the module cache, your source code, any credentials used during the build — is discarded. A Go service goes from ~850 MB to under 15 MB, and a Java service from ~600 MB (full JDK) to ~180 MB (JRE only, or less with `jlink`).

Three benefits, and the order matters when you explain them:

Security first. The runtime image has no compiler, no `curl`, no package manager, no build scripts. An attacker who gets code execution has almost nothing to pivot with — they cannot install tools, cannot compile a privilege-escalation exploit, and often cannot even get a shell. And any secret used during the build (a private-registry token, an SSH key for a private Go module) exists only in a discarded stage. This is the only reliable way to use a secret in a build without a BuildKit secret mount, because — as the layer section explained — `RUN rm secret` does not delete anything from an image.

Size second. Smaller images pull faster (which is scale-up latency and cold-start latency in Kubernetes and Lambda), cost less in registry storage and egress, and shrink your CVE surface simply by containing less software.

Maintainability third. One file, one `docker build`, no orchestration script, and the build and runtime environments are versioned together.

Things worth knowing beyond the basic pattern:

- `--target` builds a specific stage: `docker build --target=build -t app:dev .` gives you the fat image with the toolchain for local debugging, from the same Dockerfile. A very common layout is `base` → `deps` → `dev` (with test tools) → `test` (runs the suite) → `prod`, where CI runs `--target=test` and then `--target=prod`.
- BuildKit only builds the stages the target depends on. With the classic builder every stage ran in order; with BuildKit, unreferenced stages are skipped and independent stages run in parallel. A Dockerfile with separate `frontend-build` and `backend-build` stages compiles both simultaneously.
- `COPY --from` accepts a stage name, a stage index, or an external image: `COPY --from=ghcr.io/org/certs:1 /ca.pem /etc/ssl/` pulls straight from a registry without a stage.
- Running tests inside the build couples "the image built" to "the tests passed": add a stage `FROM build AS test` with `RUN go test ./...`. Because BuildKit skips unreferenced stages, you must actually target it or reference it, or it will not run.
- Watch what you copy. `COPY --from=build /src /app` copies the whole source tree back in and undoes the point of the exercise. Copy the artefact, not the workspace.
- Runtime dependencies still have to be there. A dynamically linked binary built against Debian's glibc will not run on Alpine (musl) or on `scratch`. Either build statically, or make the runtime stage the same distro family as the build stage, or copy the shared libraries too (fragile). `ldd ./binary` in the build stage tells you what you actually need.
- Non-code artefacts get forgotten: CA certificates for outbound TLS, timezone data, `/etc/passwd` if you reference a user by name, and any static assets or templates your app loads at runtime.

A crisp way to state the whole idea in an interview: the build environment and the runtime environment have almost disjoint requirements, and a multi-stage build lets you express both in one file while shipping only the second.

# Go: 850 MB toolchain -> ~12 MB image. Build, test, and ship in one file.

COPY go.mod go.sum ./
RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/go/pkg/mod go mod download
COPY . .
RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/go/pkg/mod \
    --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.cache/go-build \
    CGO_ENABLED=0 GOOS=linux \
    go build -trimpath -ldflags="-s -w -X main.version=${GIT_SHA:-dev}" \
             -o /out/server ./cmd/server

RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/go/pkg/mod \
    --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.cache/go-build \
    go vet ./... && go test -race -count=1 ./...

sections.title: 11. Base Images: scratch, distroless, alpine, slim — and the Traps in Each
sections.content:
Once you have a multi-stage build, the question becomes what to put in the final stage. The options form a spectrum from "nothing at all" to "a full distro", and each point has a specific tradeoff that interviewers like to probe because it exposes whether you have actually operated these things.

`FROM scratch` — a completely empty filesystem. No shell, no libc, no `/etc`, no CA certificates, not even `/tmp`. Your binary must be statically linked and must not assume any file exists. It works beautifully for Go and Rust, and it is the smallest and most attack-resistant option: the image is literally your binary and nothing else, so there is no `sh` to spawn, no `curl` to download a payload, no package manager. The things people forget:
- CA certificates. Any outbound HTTPS call fails with `x509: certificate signed by unknown authority` until you `COPY --from=build /etc/ssl/certs/ca-certificates.crt /etc/ssl/certs/`.
- `/etc/passwd`. `USER appuser` needs a passwd entry; either use a numeric UID or copy a minimal passwd file in.
- Timezone data. `TZ=Europe/London` silently does nothing without `/usr/share/zoneinfo`. In Go, `import _ "time/tzdata"` embeds the database into the binary instead.
- `/tmp`. Nothing exists to write to; mount a tmpfs or create the directory in the build stage and copy it.

Go and static linking specifically, because this is asked constantly: Go produces a static binary unless cgo is involved, and by default cgo is used by the `net` and `os/user` packages on Linux so they can call glibc's NSS for DNS and user lookups. `CGO_ENABLED=0` switches to the pure-Go resolver and gives you a genuinely static binary. If you must keep cgo (SQLite, some crypto libraries), either build with `-tags osusergo,netgo` and static linking flags, or accept a distro base. The tell that you got it wrong is a container that exits immediately with `no such file or directory` on a binary that visibly exists — that message is the dynamic loader (`/lib64/ld-linux-x86-64.so.2`) being missing, not your binary.

Distroless (`gcr.io/distroless/*`) is Google's middle ground: glibc, CA certificates, tzdata, `/etc/passwd`, and language runtime where applicable — but no shell, no package manager, no coreutils. `static` (~2 MB) for static binaries, `base` (~20 MB) for dynamically linked ones, plus `cc`, `java*`, `nodejs*`, `python3` variants. Every image has a `:nonroot` tag that defaults to UID 65532, and a `:debug` tag that adds a busybox shell — the standard practice is to ship the non-debug tag and swap to `:debug` only when you need to get inside. The value proposition is a near-empty CVE surface (no shell means no shellshock-class issues, and vulnerability scanners report a handful of findings instead of hundreds) with none of scratch's missing-file surprises.

Alpine (`alpine:3.20`, ~7 MB) is a real, if minimal, distro: busybox userland, `apk` package manager, and musl libc instead of glibc. It is small and convenient, and the musl swap is where the traps live:
- Python is the big one. PyPI's precompiled `manylinux` wheels are built against glibc and will not install on Alpine, so `pip install` falls back to compiling from source. Your build goes from 30 seconds to 15 minutes, needs `build-essential` and headers, and the resulting image is frequently larger than the `-slim` Debian one you were avoiding. Some projects publish `musllinux` wheels now, but coverage is far from complete. For Python, `python:3.12-slim-bookworm` is usually the better default.
- DNS behaviour differs. musl's resolver has historically diverged from glibc's in ways that bite in Kubernetes: it queries configured nameservers in parallel rather than sequentially, and older musl versions did not fall back to TCP for responses over 512 bytes, causing truncated-response failures. TCP fallback landed in musl 1.2.4 (2023), so modern Alpine is much better, but "Alpine has weird DNS in k8s" is folklore rooted in real bugs.
- Threads. musl's default thread stack size is far smaller than glibc's, which has caused stack-overflow crashes in JVM and other thread-heavy workloads.
- Performance. musl's `malloc` is optimised for size, not throughput; allocation-heavy programs can measurably regress.

`-slim` Debian/Ubuntu variants (`python:3.12-slim`, `node:22-slim`, ~80 MB) are the pragmatic default for interpreted languages: glibc, so every prebuilt wheel and native module works, `apt` available, small enough that the difference from Alpine rarely matters against a 300 MB layer of application dependencies. Full distro images (`ubuntu`, `debian`, `python:3.12`) carry compilers and hundreds of packages you do not run, and each one is a CVE the scanner will report.

Chainguard/Wolfi images deserve a mention: minimal, glibc-based, rebuilt daily, and shipped with signatures and SBOMs, aiming at "distroless with actual package management and near-zero CVEs".

The operational cost of a minimal image is debugging, and having an answer ready is what separates a good response from a textbook one. You cannot `docker exec -it app sh` into a distroless container. The answers, in order of preference: use `kubectl debug -it pod --image=nicolaka/netshoot --target=app` to attach an ephemeral debug container sharing the target's namespaces; use `docker run --pid=container:app --network=container:app` with a toolbox image for the same effect locally; use `nsenter` from the host; or, as a fallback, redeploy the `:debug` tag. All of these work precisely because a container is just a namespaced process — you attach a second, tool-bearing process to the same namespaces.
