# =============================================================================
# See every layer of the stack on a live container
# =============================================================================
docker run -d --name demo nginx:alpine
PID=$(docker inspect -f '{{.State.Pid}}' demo)

# The process tree: dockerd is NOT the parent. The shim is.
ps -o pid,ppid,comm -p "$PID"
pstree -sp "$PID"
# systemd(1)---containerd-shim(38210)---nginx(38231)---nginx(38270)
#                    ^ note: NOT a child of dockerd. runc already exited.
pgrep -a runc || echo "runc is not running - it exits after setup"

# containerd sees the same container, one level down
sudo ctr --namespace moby containers ls | grep "$(docker inspect -f '{{.Id}}' demo | cut -c1-12)"
sudo ctr --namespace moby tasks ls

# The OCI runtime bundle: config.json is the spec the runtime consumes
CID=$(docker inspect -f '{{.Id}}' demo)
sudo cat /run/containerd/io.containerd.runtime.v2.task/moby/$CID/config.json \
  | jq '{namespaces: .linux.namespaces, caps: .process.capabilities.effective,
         cgroupsPath: .linux.cgroupsPath, readonly: .root.readonly}'

# =============================================================================
# The daemon socket IS the API. The CLI is only a client.
# =============================================================================
curl -s --unix-socket /var/run/docker.sock http://localhost/version | jq '{Version, ApiVersion}'
curl -s --unix-socket /var/run/docker.sock http://localhost/containers/json \
  | jq '.[] | {Names, Image, State}'
# Anything the CLI can do, this socket can do — including starting a privileged
# container with / mounted. Socket access == host root. Never mount it casually.

# Remote daemons, same protocol:
export DOCKER_HOST=ssh://user@buildhost      # run local CLI against a remote engine
export DOCKER_HOST=tcp://10.0.1.9:2376       # only ever with TLS client certs

# =============================================================================
# The shim keeps containers alive across a daemon restart
# =============================================================================
docker inspect -f '{{.State.StartedAt}}' demo
sudo systemctl restart docker
docker ps --filter name=demo                  # still running, same start time
# Configure this explicitly for non-Swarm hosts in /etc/docker/daemon.json:
#   { "live-restore": true }

# =============================================================================
# On a Kubernetes node: `docker ps` is empty because dockerd is not involved
# =============================================================================
# crictl (CRI-level, ships with most k8s nodes)
# sudo crictl ps
# sudo crictl pods
# sudo crictl images
# sudo crictl logs <container-id>
# sudo crictl inspect <container-id> | jq '.status.resources'
#
# nerdctl (a docker-compatible CLI for containerd)
# sudo nerdctl --namespace k8s.io ps
#
# Which runtime is a node actually using?
# kubectl get nodes -o wide     # CONTAINER-RUNTIME column: containerd://1.7.x

# =============================================================================
# Building images INSIDE a cluster, with no Docker socket
# =============================================================================
cat <<'YAML'
# Kaniko: builds in userspace inside an unprivileged pod
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata: { name: build }
spec:
  restartPolicy: Never
  containers:
    - name: kaniko
      image: gcr.io/kaniko-project/executor:latest
      args:
        - --context=git://github.com/org/repo.git#refs/heads/main
        - --dockerfile=Dockerfile
        - --destination=ghcr.io/org/app:$(GIT_SHA)
        - --cache=true
        - --cache-repo=ghcr.io/org/app-cache
      volumeMounts: [{ name: creds, mountPath: /kaniko/.docker }]
  volumes:
    - name: creds
      secret: { secretName: regcred, items: [{ key: .dockerconfigjson, path: config.json }] }
YAML
# Alternative: a shared rootless BuildKit Deployment that CI connects to with
#   docker buildx create --driver remote tcp://buildkitd.build.svc:1234

docker rm -f demo

sections.title: 19. Logs, Health, Restarts, and Resource Accounting in Production
sections.content:
Once containers are running, the operational surface is logging, health, restart behaviour, and knowing which numbers to trust. These are where day-two problems live and where SRE interviews spend their time.

Logging. The container convention is that applications write to stdout and stderr, and the platform collects them. Do not write to files inside the container — those files live in the writable layer, disappear when the container is replaced, and are invisible to your log pipeline. If you must run software that insists on files (nginx access logs, some Java frameworks), symlink them to `/dev/stdout` and `/dev/stderr`, which is exactly what the official nginx image does.

Docker's default logging driver is `json-file`, which writes to `/var/lib/docker/containers/<id>/<id>-json.log`. It has no size limit by default, and this is one of the most common ways a production host runs out of disk: a chatty service in a crash loop fills the root filesystem, and then everything on the host fails in confusing ways because the daemon, the kubelet, and the database all need to write. Always configure rotation, either per container or globally in `/etc/docker/daemon.json`:

```json
{ "log-driver": "json-file",
  "log-opts": { "max-size": "10m", "max-file": "3" } }
```
Note that this applies only to newly created containers. Other drivers: `local` (a more efficient binary format with rotation on by default), `journald`, `syslog`, `fluentd`, `awslogs`, `gcplogs`, `splunk`. A critical caveat: with most non-`json-file` drivers, `docker logs` stops working, because the daemon no longer has a local copy — logs only exist wherever you shipped them. Also, the default `json-file` driver is blocking: if the log destination stalls, writes to stdout block and your application blocks with them. `--log-opt mode=non-blocking --log-opt max-buffer-size=4m` trades log loss for availability, which is usually the right trade for a latency-sensitive service.

Two more log points worth raising: emit structured JSON so the collector does not have to guess at a format, and remember that in Kubernetes the kubelet handles rotation and the container runtime's log format is a CRI format, not Docker's — an agent configured for Docker's JSON layout will not parse it.

Health. `HEALTHCHECK` in the image or `healthcheck:` in Compose runs a command inside the container on an interval. `--start-period` gives slow-starting applications a grace window where failures do not count against `--retries`. Docker marks the container `healthy`/`unhealthy` and emits events; plain Docker does not restart an unhealthy container — Swarm does, Compose uses it for `depends_on`, and Kubernetes ignores it entirely in favour of its own probes.

The Kubernetes probe distinction is a near-guaranteed follow-up: a liveness probe failing gets the container restarted, so it must only test "is this process wedged" — a liveness probe that checks the database will restart every pod in the fleet when the database has a bad minute, turning a partial outage into a total one. A readiness probe failing removes the pod from Service endpoints without restarting it, so that is where dependency checks belong. A startup probe suppresses the other two until the app has finished booting, which is the correct fix for slow JVM starts (rather than an enormous liveness `initialDelaySeconds`).

Restart policies. `no` (default), `on-failure[:max-retries]` (restart only on a non-zero exit), `always` (restart always, including after a daemon restart or host reboot), and `unless-stopped` (like `always`, but a container you manually stopped stays stopped across a daemon restart). Docker applies exponential backoff to restarts, doubling from 100 ms, which is the same idea as Kubernetes' `CrashLoopBackOff` — a pod in `CrashLoopBackOff` is not broken by the backoff; the backoff is the symptom of a container that keeps exiting, and the diagnosis is in `kubectl logs --previous`.

Resource accounting: which numbers are real. `docker stats` reports per-container CPU and memory from cgroup counters, and there is one trap you should be ready for: the memory number is `memory.current`-derived and includes page cache. A container that read a 2 GB file shows 2 GB of "usage" while its actual anonymous memory is 100 MB. That cache is reclaimable and will be dropped under pressure rather than causing an OOM kill — so an alert on `docker stats` memory approaching the limit fires constantly and falsely. The number that predicts an OOM kill is the anon figure in `memory.stat` (and in Kubernetes, `container_memory_working_set_bytes`, which subtracts inactive file cache, is the metric to alert on — not `container_memory_usage_bytes`).

The CPU equivalent: average utilisation hides throttling. Always look at `nr_throttled` and `throttled_usec` in `cpu.stat` (`container_cpu_cfs_throttled_seconds_total` in Prometheus). A service can sit at 40% average CPU and be throttled for a quarter of every period.

And the host-level numbers a container reads are the host's. `/proc/cpuinfo`, `/proc/meminfo`, and `/proc/loadavg` are not namespaced, so `nproc`, `top`, and `free` inside a container report the machine, not the limit. Every language runtime that autosizes from those numbers gets it wrong unless it has been taught to read cgroup files: set `GOMAXPROCS` (or use `go.uber.org/automaxprocs`), rely on the JVM's container support with `MaxRAMPercentage`, size Node's `--max-old-space-size`, and pin worker counts explicitly rather than deriving them from `os.cpu_count()`.

Disk. Containers fill disks in four separate places and `docker image prune` only cleans one: images, the build cache (`docker buildx prune` — frequently tens of GB and frequently the actual culprit), volumes, and logs. `docker system df -v` shows all of them. Put `/var/lib/docker` on its own filesystem on any build host so that filling it degrades builds instead of taking down the entire machine.

# =============================================================================
# 1. LOGGING — configure rotation before it fills the disk, not after
# =============================================================================
# /etc/docker/daemon.json  (applies to NEWLY CREATED containers only; restart dockerd)
cat <<'JSON'
{
  "log-driver": "json-file",
  "log-opts": { "max-size": "10m", "max-file": "3", "compress": "true" },
  "live-restore": true,
  "default-ulimits": { "nofile": { "Name": "nofile", "Soft": 65536, "Hard": 65536 } }
}
JSON

# Per container, and non-blocking so a stalled log sink cannot stall the app
docker run -d --name api \
  --log-driver json-file \
  --log-opt max-size=10m --log-opt max-file=3 \
  --log-opt mode=non-blocking --log-opt max-buffer-size=4m \
  myorg/api:1.4.2

# Find the host's log hogs (the usual cause of a mystery full disk)
sudo du -sh /var/lib/docker/containers/*/*-json.log | sort -h | tail -10

# Reading logs
docker logs -f --since=10m --tail=200 --timestamps api
docker logs api 2>&1 | jq -c 'select(.level=="error")'   # structured logs pay off here
# WARNING: with awslogs/gcplogs/fluentd/splunk drivers, `docker logs` returns
# nothing at all. The daemon keeps no local copy.

# An app that insists on log files: symlink them out (what nginx's image does)
#   RUN ln -sf /dev/stdout /var/log/nginx/access.log \
#    && ln -sf /dev/stderr /var/log/nginx/error.log

# =============================================================================
# 2. HEALTH — and what each probe is actually allowed to check
# =============================================================================
docker run -d --name web \
  --health-cmd='wget -qO- http://localhost:8080/healthz || exit 1' \
  --health-interval=10s --health-timeout=3s \
  --health-start-period=30s --health-retries=3 \
  myorg/api:1.4.2
docker inspect --format '{{.State.Health.Status}}' web           # starting|healthy|unhealthy
docker inspect --format '{{json .State.Health.Log}}' web | jq '.[-1]'
docker events --filter event=health_status --filter container=web
# NOTE: plain Docker does NOT restart an unhealthy container. Swarm does.

cat <<'YAML'
# Kubernetes: three probes, three different jobs. Getting this wrong causes outages.
startupProbe:                 # suppresses the others until boot finishes
  httpGet: { path: /healthz, port: 8080 }
  failureThreshold: 30
  periodSeconds: 5            # allows up to 150s to start
livenessProbe:                # FAILING => RESTART. Only "am I wedged?".
  httpGet: { path: /healthz, port: 8080 }   # process-local ONLY
  periodSeconds: 10
  failureThreshold: 3
readinessProbe:               # FAILING => removed from Service endpoints, no restart.
  httpGet: { path: /ready, port: 8080 }     # THIS is where dependency checks belong
  periodSeconds: 5
# Anti-pattern: checking the database in livenessProbe. One slow DB minute and
# every replica restarts simultaneously, turning a brownout into an outage.
YAML

# =============================================================================
# 3. RESTART POLICIES
# =============================================================================
docker run -d --restart=on-failure:5 myorg/worker:1.2   # only on non-zero exit
docker run -d --restart=unless-stopped myorg/api:1.4.2  # survives reboot; respects manual stop
docker inspect --format '{{.RestartCount}} {{.State.ExitCode}}' api
# Docker backs off exponentially from 100ms. Kubernetes calls the same thing
# CrashLoopBackOff — the backoff is the SYMPTOM, not the bug.

# =============================================================================
# 4. THE NUMBERS THAT LIE, AND THE ONES THAT DO NOT
# =============================================================================
docker stats --no-stream --format \
  'table {{.Name}}\t{{.CPUPerc}}\t{{.MemUsage}}\t{{.MemPerc}}\t{{.NetIO}}\t{{.PIDS}}'
# MemUsage INCLUDES page cache. A container that merely READ a 2 GB file shows
# 2 GB. That cache is reclaimable and will NOT cause an OOM kill.

CG=/sys/fs/cgroup/system.slice/docker-$(docker inspect -f '{{.Id}}' api).scope
sudo grep -E '^(anon|file|slab) ' $CG/memory.stat   # `anon` is what predicts OOM
sudo cat $CG/memory.max $CG/memory.current
sudo cat $CG/cpu.stat | grep -E 'nr_throttled|throttled_usec'   # the p99 killer

# Prometheus equivalents, in the order you should alert on them:
#   container_memory_working_set_bytes            <- alert on THIS
#   container_memory_usage_bytes                  <- includes cache; do NOT alert on this
#   rate(container_cpu_cfs_throttled_seconds_total[5m])  <- hidden latency
#   kube_pod_container_status_last_terminated_reason{reason="OOMKilled"}

# The host numbers a container sees are the HOST's — not namespaced:
docker run --rm --cpus=1 --memory=256m alpine sh -c 'nproc; free -m | head -2'
#   16              <- the host's cores, not 1
#   Mem: 64312 ...  <- the host's RAM, not 256 MB
# Which is why you must tell the runtime the truth explicitly:
#   GOMAXPROCS / automaxprocs, -XX:MaxRAMPercentage, --max-old-space-size

# =============================================================================
# 5. DISK — four separate places, and `image prune` only cleans one
# =============================================================================
docker system df -v
docker image prune -a --filter 'until=168h'
docker builder prune --keep-storage 20GB     # the build cache; often the real culprit
docker volume ls -f dangling=true
sudo du -sh /var/lib/docker/*
# On any build host, give /var/lib/docker its own filesystem so filling it
# degrades builds instead of killing sshd, the agent, and everything else.

sections.title: 20. A Debugging Playbook: The Failure Modes You Will Actually Be Asked About
sections.content:
Interviews for SRE and platform roles almost always include a "the container won't start / the container is broken, what do you do" scenario. What they are testing is whether you have a method rather than a list of commands. The method is: read the exit code, read the logs, then interrogate the four layers (image, process, resources, network) in that order.

Exit codes carry real information. Docker reports the exit status of PID 1, and for signal deaths that is `128 + signal`:
- 0 — clean exit. If the container "stopped for no reason", this usually means the main process finished. A container is not a VM; when PID 1 exits, the container is done. The classic case is running a daemon in foreground-less mode (`nginx` without `daemon off;`, or a service that forks into the background), so PID 1 immediately returns.
- 125 — the daemon itself failed: a bad flag, a bad mount, a port already bound. The error came from `docker run`, not from your program.
- 126 — the command was found but is not executable (missing execute bit, or a directory).
- 127 — command not found. In a `scratch` or distroless image this almost always means a dynamically linked binary with no loader — the message is confusingly `no such file or directory` for a file that clearly exists, and the missing file is `/lib64/ld-linux-x86-64.so.2`. Check with `ldd`.
- 137 — SIGKILL. Two causes: the cgroup OOM killer (`docker inspect -f '{{.State.OOMKilled}}'` returns true; `dmesg` confirms), or `docker stop`'s grace period expiring because PID 1 ignored SIGTERM.
- 139 — SIGSEGV, a real crash in the process.
- 143 — SIGTERM, i.e. a normal `docker stop` where the process exited on the signal rather than handling it and exiting 0.
- 1 and other small numbers — your application's own exit status; read the logs.

"exec format error" is its own category: an architecture mismatch (an `amd64` image on `arm64` hardware — extremely common when building on Apple Silicon and deploying to x86 nodes) or a script with a missing/incorrect shebang, or CRLF line endings on a shell script written on Windows, which makes the kernel look for an interpreter named `/bin/sh\r`.

The four layers, in order.

Image. Is the entrypoint what you think it is? `docker inspect -f '{{.Config.Entrypoint}} {{.Config.Cmd}} {{.Config.User}} {{.Config.WorkingDir}}'`. Is the file actually in there? Override the entrypoint to get a shell: `docker run --rm -it --entrypoint sh myimage`, and if there is no shell, extract the filesystem instead with `docker create` + `docker export`, or browse it from the host at `/proc/<pid>/root/`. Did a mount shadow it? A bind mount of an empty directory over a path that had files in the image hides them completely.

Process. Is PID 1 what you expect (`docker exec <c> ps -ef`), or is it a shell wrapping your app? Is it receiving signals? Are there zombies piling up? Is it listening on the interface you think — `0.0.0.0:8080` versus `127.0.0.1:8080` is the difference between reachable from outside the container and not, and it is one of the most common "port mapping doesn't work" causes, because a process bound to the container's loopback cannot be reached through a DNAT rule.

Resources. Exit 137 with `OOMKilled: true` is memory. Slow-but-alive with `nr_throttled` climbing is CPU throttling. `fork: retry: Resource temporarily unavailable` is `pids.max`. `too many open files` is the `nofile` ulimit, which is set per container and does not inherit your shell's. Disk-full on the host presents as bizarre unrelated failures everywhere.

Network. Work outward: can the process reach itself inside the container (`wget localhost:8080`)? Can another container on the same network resolve and reach it by name? Is DNS working (`nslookup svc` — remember only user-defined bridges have name resolution)? Is the port published and to which address (`docker port <c>`)? Is a host firewall or the `DOCKER-USER` chain involved? `nicolaka/netshoot` attached to the target's network namespace gives you `dig`, `ss`, `tcpdump`, `curl`, `mtr` and `iperf` regardless of what the target image contains.

Debugging images with no shell deserves its own note because it is the standard follow-up to any distroless answer. The trick is always the same — attach a second process to the target's namespaces. Locally: `docker run --rm -it --pid=container:app --network=container:app nicolaka/netshoot`, then browse the target's filesystem at `/proc/1/root/`. In Kubernetes: `kubectl debug -it pod/x --image=nicolaka/netshoot --target=app`, which creates an ephemeral container in the same pod. From the host: `nsenter -t <pid> -n -p`. And to inspect an image without running it at all, `docker create` followed by `docker export | tar -tv` lists every file.

Build failures have their own patterns: a cache hit that should not have been (`--no-cache` to confirm), `--progress=plain` to see the real output instead of the collapsed TUI, a build context so large it takes minutes before the first step (missing `.dockerignore`), a `COPY` failing because the source is outside the build context (paths are relative to the context root and `..` is not allowed), and a multi-stage `COPY --from` picking up nothing because the artefact path in the earlier stage was wrong.

The last thing to say in any of these answers is what you would change so it does not happen again: log rotation configured by default, memory limits set from measured working-set plus headroom, a readiness probe that is actually about readiness, images pinned by digest, a `.dockerignore` in the template repo. Interviewers weight the prevention half heavily, because anyone can read a log.

# =============================================================================
# STEP 0 — the exit code tells you which branch of the tree to walk
# =============================================================================
docker inspect mycontainer --format '
exit={{.State.ExitCode}}
oom={{.State.OOMKilled}}
error={{.State.Error}}
restarts={{.RestartCount}}
started={{.State.StartedAt}}  finished={{.State.FinishedAt}}'

#   0    -> PID 1 finished. Is your process daemonising? (nginx needs `daemon off;`)
#   125  -> dockerd itself refused: bad flag / bad mount / port in use
#   126  -> found but not executable (no +x, or it is a directory)
#   127  -> not found; on scratch/distroless usually a MISSING DYNAMIC LOADER
#   137  -> SIGKILL: cgroup OOM, or `docker stop` timeout (PID 1 ignored SIGTERM)
#   139  -> SIGSEGV
#   143  -> SIGTERM

docker logs --tail=200 --timestamps mycontainer
docker logs --tail=200 mycontainer 2>&1 | tail -50     # stderr matters most here
docker events --since=30m --filter container=mycontainer

# =============================================================================
# EXIT 137: which kind?
# =============================================================================
docker inspect mycontainer --format '{{.State.OOMKilled}}'   # true => cgroup OOM
dmesg -T | grep -iE 'memory cgroup|oom-kill' | tail -5
# "Memory cgroup out of memory: Killed process 4711 (java) total-vm:... anon-rss:2.1G"
# If OOMKilled is FALSE and it took ~10s to die, it is the stop timeout instead:
#   your PID 1 has no SIGTERM handler (shell form CMD, or an unhandled signal).

# =============================================================================
# EXIT 127 / "no such file or directory" on a file that exists
# =============================================================================
docker run --rm --entrypoint ls myimage -l /app/server        # it IS there
docker run --rm --entrypoint /app/server myimage
#   exec /app/server: no such file or directory                <- the LOADER is missing
docker run --rm --entrypoint ldd myimage /app/server
#   linux-vdso.so.1
#   libc.so.6 => not found                                     <- there it is
# Fix: CGO_ENABLED=0 for a static build, or use distroless/base instead of scratch,
#      or match the runtime distro to the build distro (glibc vs musl!).

# "exec format error" = ARCHITECTURE MISMATCH (or a bad shebang / CRLF)
docker image inspect myimage --format '{{.Os}}/{{.Architecture}}'
docker buildx imagetools inspect ghcr.io/org/app:1.4.2 | grep -A1 Platform
file ./entrypoint.sh          # "with CRLF line terminators" => /bin/sh\r not found

# =============================================================================
# THE IMAGE LAYER: what did I actually build?
# =============================================================================
docker inspect myimage --format '
entrypoint={{.Config.Entrypoint}}
cmd={{.Config.Cmd}}
user={{.Config.User}}

interviewQA.q: What is a container, technically? Explain it without using the word 'lightweight VM'.
interviewQA.a:
A container is an ordinary Linux process (or process tree) started with three things applied to it. First, namespaces change what it can see: a private PID number space so it thinks it is PID 1 and cannot see host processes, a private mount table so its `/` is the image rather than the host's filesystem, a private network stack with its own interfaces and iptables rules, plus private hostname, IPC objects and cgroup view. Second, cgroups change what it can consume: `memory.max`, `cpu.max` and `pids.max` in a cgroup v2 node account and cap its resource usage. Third, a restricted security posture changes what it can do: most Linux capabilities are dropped (Docker keeps 14 of ~40), a seccomp BPF filter blocks around 44 syscalls, an AppArmor or SELinux profile applies, and `pivot_root` swaps the root filesystem for the image's overlay mount.

There is no `struct container` in the kernel and no isolation object — `ps aux` on the host shows the container's processes as normal processes, because they are. You can build one by hand with `unshare`, a directory, and a few writes into `/sys/fs/cgroup`; Docker's contribution is the image format, the distribution protocol, and the ergonomics, not the isolation primitives. Everything else follows from this: startup is milliseconds because there is no kernel to boot, `uname -r` reports the host kernel because there is only one, and a container escape is a kernel bug rather than a Docker bug.

interviewQA.q: Why is a container not a virtual machine? When would you actually choose a VM?
interviewQA.a:
A VM runs its own kernel on virtual hardware presented by a hypervisor using hardware virtualisation extensions; a container is a process on the host's kernel. That single difference produces everything else: a VM boots firmware then a kernel then init (seconds, hundreds of MB of guest OS overhead), a container is `clone()` plus `execve()` (milliseconds, only your process's memory). Density goes from tens per host to hundreds or thousands.

The important difference is the isolation surface. A container's boundary is the entire Linux syscall ABI — 300-plus entry points into roughly 30 million lines of C that the container can call directly. A VM's boundary is the hypervisor plus a handful of virtio devices: far smaller, far more paranoid, far more audited. Both have escapes; the base rates differ by orders of magnitude. So the honest framing is that containers isolate workloads you trust from each other's bugs and resource appetites, while VMs isolate workloads you do not trust.

Choose a VM when you need a different kernel or OS (a Windows workload, or a kernel version the host cannot run), when you need kernel modules or kernel-level tuning that would affect other tenants, when the workload is untrusted or under a hard multi-tenant compliance boundary, or when you need live migration. And it is rarely either/or: nearly every production container already runs inside a VM, because that is what an EC2 instance is. If you need VM-grade isolation at container-grade density, the middle ground is gVisor (a user-space kernel intercepting syscalls), Kata Containers (a microVM per pod behind the normal CRI interface), or Firecracker — which is exactly why AWS Lambda and Fargate run on Firecracker microVMs.

interviewQA.q: What is the difference between an image and a container?
interviewQA.a:
An image is a read-only template: an ordered list of filesystem layers plus a configuration blob describing the default entrypoint, command, environment, user, working directory and exposed ports. A container is a running or stopped instance of that image with one extra, thin, writable layer on top. One image, many containers — exactly the class-to-object or executable-to-process relationship.

Physically, an OCI image is three kinds of content-addressed object in a registry: layer blobs (compressed tars, each a diff of added/changed/deleted files relative to the layer below), a config blob (the runtime defaults plus `rootfs.diff_ids` and a build history), and a manifest tying them together. Two digests get confused: the image ID in `docker images` is the digest of the config blob, while the repo digest you pin in production (`app@sha256:...`) is the digest of the manifest.

At run time the layers are stacked by OverlayFS as read-only `lowerdir`s with a per-container writable `upperdir`, presented as one merged filesystem. Because the lower layers are immutable and content-addressed, twenty containers from the same image share exactly one copy on disk and one copy of the executable pages in the page cache — which is most of why container density is so high. When you `docker rm` a container, only that thin writable layer is deleted; the image layers stay. That is why any state you care about must be on a volume.

interviewQA.q: Explain image layers and the build cache. Why does my CI rebuild all dependencies on every commit?
interviewQA.a:
Each Dockerfile instruction that changes the filesystem produces a layer, and the builder caches them. The cache key for an instruction is the parent layer's identity plus the instruction text — and for `COPY`/`ADD`, plus a checksum of the file contents being copied. If the key matches a cached layer, the instruction is skipped. If it does not, the instruction runs and every subsequent instruction is a guaranteed miss, because their parent identity changed. Invalidation cascades downward and never recovers.

That cascade is why the answer to the question is almost always instruction ordering. The broken shape is `COPY . .` followed by `RUN npm ci`: any source change — every commit — invalidates the `COPY` layer, so the dependency install re-runs. The fix is to copy only the dependency manifests first, install, and then copy the source:

```
COPY package.json package-lock.json ./
RUN npm ci
COPY . .
```
Now the install layer's key depends only on the lockfile, so it hits the cache on the 99% of commits that do not touch dependencies. The same shape works for `go.mod`/`go.sum`, `requirements.txt`, `pom.xml`, `Cargo.toml`.

Two more causes. A missing `.dockerignore` means `.git` and `node_modules` are part of the context checksum, so the `COPY` layer changes constantly even when your source did not. And on ephemeral CI runners there is simply no local cache at all, which needs a remote one: `--cache-to type=registry,ref=repo:buildcache,mode=max` and the matching `--cache-from`, where `mode=max` matters because it exports intermediate stages too. BuildKit's `RUN --mount=type=cache` is the complementary tool: it keeps `~/.npm` or the Go module cache warm across builds without putting it in a layer, so even a genuine cache miss on the lockfile only re-links rather than re-downloading.

Finally, note that for `RUN` only the command string is hashed — the builder has no idea what the command does. `RUN apt-get update` hits the cache forever and serves a stale package index, which is why `update` and `install` must be a single `RUN`.

interviewQA.q: I have a secret in my image. I added `RUN rm /app/secret.json` after copying it in. Is the secret gone?
interviewQA.a:
No, and this is the most important thing to understand about layers. Each layer is an immutable diff, and layers below are shared and read-only. When you delete a file that exists in a lower layer, OverlayFS cannot actually remove it — it creates a whiteout: a character device with major/minor 0/0 in the writable layer (or, in the OCI tar layer format, a zero-length `.wh.<name>` file) that masks the name. The original bytes are still sitting in the earlier layer blob.

The practical consequence: the file is invisible inside a running container, so it looks fixed, but anyone who can pull the image can extract it. `docker save myimage | tar x` and then grepping the layer tarballs finds it in seconds. The image is also now larger, because you added a whiteout on top of the original content rather than removing anything. The same logic explains why `RUN apt-get purge build-essential` in a later layer does not shrink the image at all.

There are exactly two correct fixes. The first is never put it in a layer: use a BuildKit secret mount, `RUN --mount=type=secret,id=token,target=/root/.npmrc npm ci`, which mounts the secret from a tmpfs for the duration of one command and leaves it out of every layer, out of `docker history`, and out of the image metadata. The second is a multi-stage build: use the secret in a builder stage and `COPY --from=build` only the artefact, so the entire stage — and every layer in it — is discarded.

The related traps: `ARG` values passed with `--build-arg` are visible in `docker history` forever, and `ENV` values are visible in `docker inspect` to anyone who can pull the image, so neither is a secret mechanism. And if the secret already shipped, the only real remediation is to rotate it — deleting the tag does not un-pull the image from anyone who already has it.

interviewQA.q: ENTRYPOINT vs CMD — what's the difference, and which should I use?
interviewQA.a:
At container start the executed command is `ENTRYPOINT` with `CMD` appended as arguments. So `ENTRYPOINT ["ping"]` plus `CMD ["-c","3","localhost"]` runs `ping -c 3 localhost`. Anything you pass after the image name on `docker run` replaces CMD only — `docker run img example.com` gives `ping example.com` — while replacing the entrypoint needs the explicit `--entrypoint` flag. With no ENTRYPOINT, CMD is the whole command.

So the choice is about intent. Use `ENTRYPOINT` when the image is a program and you want `docker run myimage --flag` to feel like invoking it; use `CMD` alone when the image is an environment and `docker run myimage bash` should work naturally. `CMD` as default arguments under an `ENTRYPOINT` is the idiomatic combination. One sharp edge: setting `ENTRYPOINT` in a Dockerfile resets any inherited `CMD` to empty, so you must re-specify it.

The bigger issue is exec form versus shell form, and it is a production bug rather than a style preference. `CMD python app.py` (shell form) is rewritten to `["/bin/sh","-c","python app.py"]`, which makes `/bin/sh` PID 1 with your app as its child. When `docker stop` sends SIGTERM to PID 1, the shell has no handler and does not forward it; your app never learns to shut down, Docker escalates to SIGKILL after the 10-second grace period, in-flight requests are dropped, and you get exit code 137. Shell form also breaks argument passing, since extra `docker run` args become arguments to `sh`, not to your program. Some shells opportunistically `exec` a single simple command and accidentally save you, but that disappears the moment your command contains `&&`, a pipe, or a redirect.

So: exec form, always, for both. If you genuinely need shell features, write the shell explicitly and write the `exec` yourself: `ENTRYPOINT ["/bin/sh","-c","exec myapp --port ${PORT}"]`. And the standard wrapper-script pattern — `ENTRYPOINT ["/entrypoint.sh"]` with `CMD` as the default command — depends entirely on the script's last line being `exec "$@"`, so that your process replaces the shell and becomes PID 1.

interviewQA.q: What is special about PID 1 inside a container, and why does `docker run --init` exist?
interviewQA.a:
In a PID namespace the first process gets kernel treatment that no other process gets, and it causes two distinct production bugs.

Signals. For PID 1, the kernel's default signal dispositions do not apply. Any signal other than SIGKILL and SIGSTOP for which PID 1 has not installed a handler is simply discarded — including from the host, which is where `docker stop` sends it from. Normally SIGTERM's default action terminates a process; for PID 1 it does nothing at all. So a shell, or a script, or any program that never registered a SIGTERM handler, is effectively immune to `docker stop`: it sits there for the whole grace period (10 seconds by default) and is then SIGKILLed, exit 137, with no graceful drain and no chance to close connections.

Zombie reaping. When a process's parent dies, the orphan is reparented to PID 1 of its namespace, and PID 1 is responsible for calling `wait()` on it. Most application runtimes never do. In a container whose main process shells out frequently — a CI agent, a job runner, anything invoking subprocesses — orphaned children accumulate as `<defunct>` entries, each holding a PID slot, until you hit `pids.max` or the host's PID limit and `fork()` starts failing across the box.

A third, less subtle one: if PID 1 exits, the entire namespace is torn down and every other process in the container is killed immediately.

`docker run --init` inserts `tini` as PID 1. Tini does two jobs and nothing else: it forwards signals to your process, and it reaps orphaned children. You can also bake it in with `ENTRYPOINT ["/sbin/tini","--","myapp"]`, or use `dumb-init`. You need it whenever your PID 1 is a shell script, a supervisor, or a runtime that spawns and abandons children. If your application handles SIGTERM properly and does not orphan processes, you do not need it — the best answer is to make your app a well-behaved PID 1, and use an init when you cannot.

Worth adding: `STOPSIGNAL` in the Dockerfile changes which signal `docker stop` sends, which matters for images like nginx that want SIGQUIT for a graceful drain rather than SIGTERM's fast shutdown.

interviewQA.q: What is a multi-stage build and what problem does it solve?
interviewQA.a:
A multi-stage build puts several `FROM` instructions in one Dockerfile, each starting a fresh stage, and uses `COPY --from=<stage>` to pull artefacts across. Only the layers of the final stage end up in the image; every earlier stage is discarded.

The problems it solves, in order of importance:

Security. The runtime image has no compiler, no package manager, no build scripts, and often no shell. An attacker with code execution has almost nothing to pivot with. And any credential used during the build — a private registry token, an SSH key for a private module — lives only in a discarded stage. This matters because, as the layer model dictates, `RUN rm secret` does not actually remove anything from an image; discarding the whole stage does.

Size. A Go service goes from ~850 MB with the toolchain to under 15 MB on distroless or scratch. A Java service from ~600 MB with a JDK to ~110 MB with a jlink'd runtime. That is scale-up latency in Kubernetes, cold-start time in serverless, registry storage, and egress cost — plus a smaller CVE surface simply because there is less software present.

Maintainability. One file, one `docker build`, build and runtime environments versioned together, instead of two Dockerfiles glued by a shell script that `docker cp`s artefacts between them.

Things worth mentioning beyond the basics: `--target` builds a named stage, so the same Dockerfile gives you `--target=dev` with debugging tools and `--target=prod` for release, and a `FROM build AS test` stage running `go test` lets CI couple "the image built" to "the tests passed". BuildKit only builds the stages the target depends on and runs independent stages in parallel, so separate frontend and backend build stages compile simultaneously. `COPY --from` also accepts an external image reference, not just a stage.

The traps: copy the artefact, not the workspace (`COPY --from=build /src /app` undoes the whole point); a dynamically linked binary built on Debian will not run on Alpine or scratch, so either build statically or match the libc; and remember the non-code things that scratch does not have — CA certificates, tzdata, `/etc/passwd`.

interviewQA.q: scratch vs distroless vs alpine vs slim — how do you choose a base image?
interviewQA.a:
It is a spectrum from "nothing" to "a full distro", and the choice depends on the language and on how much debuggability you are willing to trade.

`scratch` is an empty filesystem — no shell, no libc, no `/etc`, no CA certificates, not even `/tmp`. It requires a statically linked binary and is ideal for Go and Rust. It is the smallest and most attack-resistant option, because there is literally no `sh` to spawn and no `curl` to fetch a payload. The four things people forget: copy `ca-certificates.crt` or every outbound HTTPS call fails with `x509: certificate signed by unknown authority`; copy `/etc/passwd` (or use a numeric UID) if you reference a user by name; copy zoneinfo (or in Go, `import _ "time/tzdata"`) or `TZ` silently does nothing; and create `/tmp` if anything needs scratch space.

Distroless (`gcr.io/distroless/*`) is the pragmatic middle: glibc, CA certificates, tzdata and `/etc/passwd`, but no shell and no package manager. There are `static`, `base`, `cc`, `java*`, `nodejs*` and `python3` variants, each with a `:nonroot` tag defaulting to UID 65532 and a `:debug` tag that adds busybox. You get scratch's near-empty CVE report without scratch's missing-file surprises. This is my default for compiled languages.

Alpine (~7 MB) is a real distro on musl libc, and the libc swap is where the traps are. For Python it is usually a mistake: PyPI's precompiled `manylinux` wheels are glibc-built and will not install, so `pip install` compiles from source — a 30-second build becomes 15 minutes, you have to add a toolchain, and the result is often larger than the Debian slim image you were avoiding. musl's DNS resolver has historically diverged from glibc's in ways that bite in Kubernetes (parallel queries, and no TCP fallback for large responses until musl 1.2.4). Its default thread stack is much smaller, which has crashed JVM workloads, and its allocator trades throughput for size.

`-slim` Debian variants are the sane default for interpreted languages: glibc so every prebuilt wheel and native module works, `apt` available for the two runtime libraries you need, and typically ~80 MB before your dependencies — which are usually far larger than the base anyway. Full distro images carry compilers and hundreds of unused packages, each of which is a CVE the scanner will report.

The cost of going minimal is debugging, and having an answer ready matters: you cannot `docker exec -it app sh` into a distroless container. The fix is to attach a second process to the target's namespaces — `kubectl debug --target=app --image=nicolaka/netshoot` in Kubernetes, `docker run --pid=container:app --network=container:app netshoot` locally, or `nsenter` from the host — which works precisely because a container is just a namespaced process.

interviewQA.q: Volumes vs bind mounts vs tmpfs — when do you use each, and what goes wrong?
interviewQA.a:
Named volumes are Docker-managed storage referenced by name, living under `/var/lib/docker/volumes/<name>/_data` on Linux but addressed by name, not path. They survive `docker rm`, can move between containers, can be backed by a plugin driver, and — a detail people miss — if the volume is empty on first use, Docker copies the image's content at that path into it. That is how `-v html:/usr/share/nginx/html nginx` gives you a volume pre-seeded with nginx's default page. This is the right choice for application state on a single host, and on Docker Desktop they are dramatically faster than bind mounts because the data stays inside the Linux VM.

Bind mounts map a host path straight in. No management, no pre-seeding — and an empty host directory shadows whatever the image had at that path, which is the "my config files disappeared" bug. They are right for development (live source reload), for injecting configuration, and for read-only mounts of host data; wrong for production state, because they hard-code a host path and pin the container to one machine. Two traps: ownership is enforced by numeric UID with no translation across the boundary, so a container running as UID 10001 writing into a host directory owned by 1000 gets `EACCES` — the fix is to align the numbers, not `chmod 777`, and on SELinux hosts you also need the `:z` or `:Z` relabel suffix. And with the short `-v` syntax, a nonexistent host path is silently created as an empty root-owned directory, so a typo produces a mystery rather than an error. `--mount type=bind` errors instead, which is why I prefer `--mount`.

tmpfs is RAM-backed and vanishes with the container. It is the right answer for scratch space and for secrets that should not touch disk, and it is what makes `--read-only` practical: mount the rootfs read-only and hand back a small tmpfs for `/tmp` and `/run`. The trap is that tmpfs pages are charged to the container's memory cgroup — a container with `--memory=256m` that writes 300 MB to a tmpfs gets OOM-killed.

Two more points I would raise unprompted. `VOLUME` in a Dockerfile is almost always a mistake: it creates a new anonymous volume on every `docker run` that nobody cleans up, and any `RUN` after it writing to that path has its changes silently discarded. And this is all single-host: in a cluster, a named volume is node-local and a rescheduled pod loses it, so the real answer is a PersistentVolumeClaim backed by a CSI driver — or, for a database, seriously considering a managed service instead.

interviewQA.q: Walk me through Docker's default bridge networking. What happens when I run `-p 8080:80`?
interviewQA.a:
Three pieces: a network namespace per container, a veth pair connecting it to a Linux bridge on the host, and iptables NAT rules at the edge.

Docker creates a bridge — `docker0` for the default network, typically `172.17.0.0/16`. For each container it creates a veth pair, a virtual patch cable: one end goes into the container's network namespace and is renamed `eth0`, the other stays on the host and is enslaved to the bridge. The container gets an address from the subnet and a default route via the bridge IP. Outbound traffic is source-NATed by a `MASQUERADE` rule in the `nat` table's `POSTROUTING` chain, so it leaves with the host's address.

`-p 8080:80` adds inbound reachability: a DNAT rule in the `nat` table's `DOCKER` chain rewrites the destination of packets arriving on host port 8080 to `172.17.0.2:80`, plus a small `docker-proxy` userland process that covers the loopback and hairpin cases the kernel rules do not. Note that `EXPOSE` in a Dockerfile publishes nothing — it is metadata that `-P` and some tooling read.

Two things I would add unprompted. First, the default bridge has no DNS between containers — you get IPs and the deprecated `--link`. A user-defined bridge (`docker network create mynet`) gets Docker's embedded DNS at 127.0.0.11, resolving container names and aliases to their current IPs, and since IPs change on every restart that is the only sane way for containers to find each other. User-defined bridges are also isolated from one another. Compose creates one per project automatically, which is why service names just work there.

Second, the firewall bypass. Docker's DNAT happens in `nat/PREROUTING`, and the packet then traverses `FORWARD` — it never reaches `filter/INPUT`, which is where `ufw` and most host firewall configurations put their rules. So you can `ufw deny 5432`, publish Postgres with `-p 5432:5432`, and have your database on the public internet anyway. This has ransomwared a great many databases. The fixes are to publish to loopback (`-p 127.0.0.1:5432:5432`) or a private interface, to not publish at all and put the database on an internal network only the app can reach, or to filter in the `DOCKER-USER` chain, which exists specifically so your rules run before Docker's.

interviewQA.q: Compare Docker's network modes: bridge, host, none, container, macvlan, overlay.
interviewQA.a:
bridge is the default: a private network namespace, a veth pair to a Linux bridge, NAT for egress and DNAT for published ports. It gives port isolation and, on a user-defined bridge, name-based DNS. It costs you a NAT hop, which matters only at very high packet rates.

host (`--network=host`) skips the network namespace entirely — the container uses the host's interfaces, addresses and ports directly. No NAT, no veth, and `-p` is silently ignored because there is nothing to map. Use it when NAT overhead genuinely matters or when a process must see the host's real network (a monitoring agent, a DHCP client, a load balancer doing direct return). Costs: no port isolation, so two containers cannot both bind 8080, and binding a port binds it on the host. On Docker Desktop the "host" is the Linux VM, not your Mac, so it does not do what people expect.

none gives a namespace with only a down loopback. Right for batch jobs that must not touch the network.

`container:<name>` joins an existing container's network namespace: both see the same interfaces and reach each other on `localhost`. This is precisely how a Kubernetes Pod is built — the kubelet creates a sandbox ("pause") container that owns the netns and every container in the pod joins it, which is why pod containers share an IP and talk over localhost. It is also the standard way to attach a debug toolbox to a container that has no tools.

macvlan / ipvlan put the container directly on the physical LAN with its own MAC (macvlan) or the host's MAC and a distinct IP (ipvlan). No NAT, the container is a first-class device on the network — useful for legacy applications needing a real LAN address or for broadcast/multicast protocols. Costs: the switch port usually needs promiscuous mode, most cloud providers forbid it, and by default the host cannot reach its own macvlan containers, which needs an extra shim interface to work around.

overlay spans hosts by encapsulating frames in VXLAN over UDP 4789, giving containers on different machines one L2 domain; it needs a control plane to distribute endpoint state, which Swarm provides. The classic operational failure is MTU: VXLAN adds 50 bytes, so the effective MTU drops to 1450, and if you leave it at 1500 you get the maddening symptom of handshakes and small requests working while large responses hang — full-size segments are silently dropped, especially where a firewall blocks the ICMP that Path MTU Discovery needs.
followUps: Why would you ever use host networking, and what do you give up?
Explain the MTU problem with overlay networks and how you would diagnose it.
Why can't the host reach its own macvlan containers by default?

interviewQA.q: How does Docker Compose work, and would you run it in production?
interviewQA.a:
Compose reads a YAML file describing services, networks and volumes and brings them up as a unit on one host. `docker compose up` derives a project name (the directory name by default), creates a user-defined bridge called `<project>_default`, and joins every service to it, so services reach each other by service name through Docker's embedded DNS. Containers and volumes get the project prefix, which is what lets the same stack run twice on one machine. Note the history: Compose v1 was the Python `docker-compose`; v2 is the Go plugin `docker compose`, and the `version:` key at the top of the file is obsolete in the Compose Specification.

The gotcha I always call out is that `depends_on` does not mean ready. By default it only controls start order — the database container is started, then yours, with no regard for whether Postgres has finished initialising. Your app connects, gets connection refused, and crashes. The correct form pairs a `healthcheck` on the dependency with `depends_on: { db: { condition: service_healthy } }`; the conditions are `service_started`, `service_healthy`, and `service_completed_successfully` for one-shot migration containers. Even then, a production-grade service should retry its own connections, because no real orchestrator guarantees ordering.

The other thing people conflate is environment handling: a file literally named `.env` supplies values for `${VAR}` interpolation inside the Compose file — it configures Compose — while `env_file:` lists files whose contents become environment variables inside the container. They are unrelated.

Would I run it in production? For a single-host, low-stakes deployment where losing that host is acceptable — a small internal tool, a side project, a staging environment — yes, and plenty of systems do exactly that, with `restart: unless-stopped`, log rotation, resource limits and a healthcheck. But Compose orchestrates one machine: there is no scheduling across nodes, no rescheduling when a host dies, no health-gated rolling update, no autoscaling, no secrets management beyond files, and the `deploy:` keys are largely ignored outside Swarm. The moment you need multi-node availability or zero-downtime deploys, you need a real orchestrator. The good news is that the images are identical either way, so the migration is a rewrite of the orchestration layer, not of the application — and Compose remains the right tool for local development and CI integration tests alongside whatever runs in production.
followUps: How do you make one service actually wait until another is ready?
What is the difference between the `.env` file and `env_file:`?
What exactly does `docker compose down -v` do, and why is it dangerous?

interviewQA.q: My container was killed with exit code 137. Walk me through diagnosing it.
interviewQA.a:
137 is 128 + 9, so PID 1 died on SIGKILL. There are two distinct causes and the first job is to tell them apart.

`docker inspect <id> --format '{{.State.OOMKilled}}'` — if that is true, the cgroup memory limit was hit. `dmesg -T | grep -i 'memory cgroup'` confirms it with the killed process, its RSS, and the limit. The critical thing to say here is that this is a per-cgroup event: the host can have 200 GB free and this is still perfectly normal, because `memory.max` applies to the group, not the machine. The kernel tried to reclaim within the cgroup first — dropping clean page cache, swapping if allowed — and only killed when reclaim could not free enough.

If `OOMKilled` is false and the container took roughly ten seconds to die after a stop or a redeploy, it is the `docker stop` grace period instead: SIGTERM went to PID 1, PID 1 had no handler and (because of PID 1's special semantics) the kernel discarded it, and Docker escalated to SIGKILL after the default 10 seconds. That is a signal-handling bug, usually shell-form `CMD` putting `/bin/sh` at PID 1, and the fix is exec form plus a real SIGTERM handler, or `--init`.

For the OOM branch, the root cause is usually one of four things. A runtime that autosized from host memory: `/proc/meminfo` is not namespaced, so a JVM without container support, or a Node process without `--max-old-space-size`, or a worker pool sized from `os.cpu_count()`, computes its budget from the machine's RAM and blows past the limit. A genuine leak, which shows as `anon` in `memory.stat` climbing monotonically across restarts. Uncounted memory: tmpfs and `/dev/shm` writes are charged to the cgroup, so a container writing 300 MB to `/tmp` under a 256 MB limit dies even though its heap is small. A limit set too low from a guess rather than from measurement.

The measurement point matters: `docker stats` memory includes page cache, so a container that merely read a large file shows huge "usage" that is reclaimable and will never cause a kill. The number that predicts an OOM is `anon` in `memory.stat` — in Kubernetes, `container_memory_working_set_bytes`, not `container_memory_usage_bytes`. Alerting on the wrong one is why so many memory alerts are noise.

The fix is to measure the working set under realistic load, set the limit to that plus headroom, and then tell the runtime the truth: `-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75`, `GOMEMLIMIT`, `--max-old-space-size`. And if the OOM killed a worker child rather than PID 1, the container survives in a degraded state — which is why your healthcheck needs to actually exercise the application, not just check that a port is open.
followUps: Why does `docker stats` show memory usage far above what the app allocated?
How does the JVM decide its max heap inside a container, and what changed in JDK 10?
What if exit code 137 comes with OOMKilled: false?

interviewQA.q: A service is slow but its CPU usage looks fine — around 40%. What could be happening?
interviewQA.a:
The first thing I would check is CFS throttling, because average CPU utilisation hides it completely.

A CPU limit (`--cpus=1`, or a Kubernetes CPU limit) is enforced as a quota per period: `cpu.max` of `100000 100000` means 100 ms of CPU time per 100 ms of wall clock. Crucially, that quota is consumed by all runnable threads together. A JVM or Go service with 40 threads on a 16-core box can burn the entire 100 ms budget in the first ~10 ms of the period — and then every thread in the cgroup is descheduled until the next period boundary. The application is frozen for 90 ms. Averaged over the period, utilisation reads as a comfortable 10-40%; p99 latency has a 90 ms cliff in it that no CPU graph will show you.

The evidence is in `cpu.stat`: `nr_throttled` and `throttled_usec`. In Prometheus it is `rate(container_cpu_cfs_throttled_seconds_total[5m])`. If those are non-zero and rising, that is your answer, and no amount of profiling application code will find it.

Three fixes, with real tradeoffs. Raise the limit — simple, but you are now reserving capacity you use in bursts. Reduce parallelism to match the limit: this is the underrated one, because a container that thinks it has 16 CPUs will size its thread pools, GC threads and connection pools for 16 CPUs. `/proc/cpuinfo` is not namespaced, so you must tell the runtime explicitly — `GOMAXPROCS` (or `go.uber.org/automaxprocs`, which reads the cgroup), `-XX:ActiveProcessorCount`, an explicit worker count instead of `os.cpu_count()`. Fewer threads means less contention and far less throttling. Remove the CPU limit and rely on requests plus `cpu.weight` for isolation, which is a genuinely contested position in the Kubernetes community: you get much better tail latency and lose hard predictability of noisy-neighbour behaviour. Many teams run with memory limits and no CPU limits for exactly this reason.

If throttling is not the cause, the other candidates in a container context are: the container is on a node whose other containers are saturating the CPU (check node-level pressure, not just this container), block I/O contention from `io.max` or a shared disk, network latency that CPU graphs will never show, and the classic non-container answer that the service is blocked on a downstream dependency and CPU is low precisely because it is waiting.
followUps: Why does reducing GOMAXPROCS help when the container is throttled?
What is the difference between cpu.weight and cpu.max, and which one does `--cpus` set?
Would you set CPU limits on your Kubernetes pods? Argue both sides.

interviewQA.q: How do you keep container images small and secure? What do vulnerability scanners actually see?
interviewQA.a:
Size and security are largely the same problem: both are functions of shipping software you do not run.

For size, measure before you optimise — `docker history --no-trunc` for per-instruction sizes, `dive` for a layer browser that flags files added in one layer and deleted in another. The usual causes in order: the build toolchain in the runtime image (fix: multi-stage), package caches left behind (delete in the same `RUN`, or better, use `RUN --mount=type=cache` so they never enter a layer), dev dependencies, `.git` and test data pulled in by `COPY . .` with no `.dockerignore`, and a `RUN chown -R` after a big `COPY` which duplicates every touched file into a new layer (fix: `COPY --chown=`).

Scanners — Trivy, Grype, Docker Scout — work by unpacking the layers, finding the package databases (`/var/lib/dpkg/status`, the RPM DB, `/lib/apk/db/installed`), reading out installed package name/version pairs, additionally parsing language lockfiles they find (`package-lock.json`, `poetry.lock`, `go.mod`, JAR manifests), and matching all of that against vulnerability feeds. Understanding that mechanism tells you what they miss: anything not in a package database — a dependency you `curl`-ed and untarred, or built from source — is invisible; statically linked C libraries compiled into a binary are invisible (Go is a partial exception, since the toolchain embeds module metadata that Trivy reads); and your own code's bugs are entirely out of scope, that is SAST territory. It also explains why distroless collapses the report: with no shell, no coreutils and no package manager, there are barely any OS packages left to have CVEs — which is a real reduction in attack surface but says nothing about your application's dependencies.

Triage is the actual skill. A stock `ubuntu:22.04` reports dozens of findings, most unreachable in context. A defensible policy is: fail the build on fixable critical and high findings, allow time-boxed exceptions with expiry dates, and — the highest-leverage item by far — rebuild regularly, because most findings are resolved by a newer base image rather than by any change to your code. A weekly automated rebuild-and-redeploy of unchanged services removes more risk than most scanning policies do.

Then the supply-chain layer: generate an SBOM so the next Log4Shell is an inventory query rather than 400 rescans; produce provenance attestations recording the source commit and builder; sign with cosign, ideally keylessly so the signature binds to your CI's OIDC identity in a transparency log rather than to a key someone has to rotate; and enforce it with admission control (Kyverno or a Sigstore policy controller) so the cluster refuses anything not signed by your pipeline. Finally, a perfect image can still be run badly: non-root user, read-only rootfs, `--cap-drop=ALL`, `no-new-privileges`, resource limits, no Docker socket, and network policy — enforced by admission policy, not by hoping every team remembers.
followUps: Why does switching to distroless drop your CVE count so dramatically, and what does it NOT fix?
What is an SBOM for, in practice? Give a concrete scenario.
How would you stop unsigned images from running in a Kubernetes cluster?

interviewQA.q: What is the difference between a tag and a digest, and how should you reference images in production?
interviewQA.a:
A tag is a mutable pointer in a registry: `myapp:1.4.2` is a name that can be reassigned to different content at any time, by anyone with push access. A digest (`myapp@sha256:...`) is the content hash of the manifest; it is immutable by construction, because different content produces a different hash. `latest` is not special in any way — it is just the conventional default tag, with no notion of recency, and an image tagged `latest` may be a year old.

The failure this causes in production: you deploy `myapp:latest`. Node A pulled it an hour ago and has it cached; node B scales up now and pulls a rebuilt image. You are running two different builds behind the same load balancer, with different behaviour, and nothing in your deployment history records that anything changed. Kubernetes' `imagePullPolicy` papers over this inconsistently — it defaults to `Always` for `:latest` and `IfNotPresent` for a pinned tag — which makes the behaviour harder to reason about rather than easier.

The rule I would state: build with an immutable tag and deploy by digest. Immutable tags carry meaning for humans — `1.4.2`, or `sha-a3f9c21` from the commit — and most registries (ECR, GAR, GHCR, Harbor) can enforce tag immutability as a setting, which you should turn on. Then resolve that tag to a digest in CI and put the digest in the deployment manifest. You get a human-readable audit trail and a byte-exact guarantee of what is running. The same argument applies to your base images: pin `FROM` by digest and let Renovate or Dependabot bump it as a reviewable pull request, so you get reproducible builds and patches, but never a silent change.

Worth adding: the digest is also what signatures and attestations bind to. `cosign sign` signs a digest, not a tag, precisely because a tag could be moved afterwards — so any verification policy that checks a tag is not actually verifying anything.

And one related concept: what a tag points at may be an image index (manifest list) rather than a single manifest, containing per-platform entries. That is how `docker pull alpine` gives you arm64 on an M-series Mac and amd64 in CI from the same tag. `docker buildx imagetools inspect <ref>` shows which platforms an index contains — and checking that is how you avoid the `exec format error` that follows from pushing a single-arch image built on Apple Silicon to x86 nodes.
followUps: How does Kubernetes' imagePullPolicy interact with tags versus digests?
How do you build a multi-architecture image, and how does the client pick the right one?
If you pin everything by digest, how do you still get security patches?

interviewQA.q: What happens, end to end, when you run `docker run nginx`? Name the components.
interviewQA.a:
The `docker` CLI is only an HTTP client. It sends a request to the Docker Engine API over the Unix socket `/var/run/docker.sock` (or TCP, or SSH via `DOCKER_HOST`). Nothing the CLI does is privileged in itself — which is exactly why socket access is equivalent to host root, since anyone who can talk to it can start a privileged container with `/` mounted.

`dockerd`, the daemon, handles the high-level product surface: resolving the image reference, the build API, networking through libnetwork (creating the bridge, the veth pair, the iptables rules, the embedded DNS), volumes, logging drivers, restart policies. It does not create containers itself.

It calls `containerd` over gRPC. containerd is the container supervisor — a CNCF project Docker donated — responsible for pulling and unpacking images through snapshotters, managing the content store, and supervising container lifecycle.

containerd starts a `containerd-shim-runc-v2` process, one per container. This is the piece people forget and it exists for a specific reason: the shim becomes the container's parent, holds its stdio/pty, and reports its exit status, so containerd and dockerd can be restarted or upgraded without killing running containers. That is why `systemctl restart docker` does not stop your workloads.

The shim invokes `runc`, the OCI runtime. runc reads an OCI runtime bundle — a root filesystem plus a `config.json` describing namespaces, cgroups, mounts, capabilities, seccomp and the LSM label — then does the actual kernel work: `clone()` with the namespace flags, set up the cgroup, mount `/proc`, `/sys` and the overlay, `pivot_root`, apply capabilities and the seccomp filter, and `execve` the entrypoint. Then runc exits. It is not a daemon; while your container runs, its parent is the shim, not runc.

The three OCI specifications are what make this modular: the image spec (manifests, configs, layers), the runtime spec (the bundle and the create/start/kill/delete operations), and the distribution spec (the registry HTTP API). Because they are standards, the pieces swap: runc can be replaced by crun, youki, gVisor's `runsc`, or kata-runtime; containerd by CRI-O; and an image built by Buildah runs fine under containerd.

That modularity is also the answer to the "Kubernetes deprecated Docker" story. The kubelet talks to runtimes through the CRI; Docker never implemented it, so Kubernetes carried an adapter called dockershim, deprecated in 1.20 and removed in 1.24. Kubernetes now calls containerd directly, cutting out two hops. Your images are unaffected — they are OCI images. What broke was anything depending on the daemon being on the node: mounting the Docker socket to build images (use Kaniko or a remote BuildKit), the `docker` CLI for node debugging (use `crictl` or `nerdctl`), and log agents parsing Docker's JSON log format.
followUps: Why does restarting dockerd not kill running containers?
What is runc actually doing, syscall by syscall?
Kubernetes removed dockershim in 1.24 — what actually broke for users, and what didn't?

interviewQA.q: Why is mounting `/var/run/docker.sock` into a container dangerous? What do you do instead?
interviewQA.a:
Because the Docker socket is the full Engine API with no authorisation layer. Anyone who can write to it can do anything the daemon can do, and the daemon runs as root on the host. The escape is one command: start a new container with `--privileged` and the host's `/` bind-mounted, then `chroot` into it. You now have a root shell on the host, with access to every other container's filesystem, every secret on the node, and the kubelet's credentials if it is a Kubernetes node. Mounting the socket is therefore functionally identical to handing out the host root password — and it is worse than it looks, because it is usually done casually, to a CI runner or a monitoring agent or a "Docker management UI", where a single supply-chain compromise in any dependency of that container becomes full host compromise.

The same reasoning covers the neighbouring anti-patterns: `--privileged` (all capabilities, no seccomp, no AppArmor, all host devices), bind-mounting sensitive host paths, `--pid=host` with `CAP_SYS_PTRACE` (read any host process's memory), and running as root inside the container so that any RCE starts at UID 0 — which, without user namespaces, is UID 0 on the host.

What to do instead depends on why the socket was wanted:
- Building images in CI — use a rootless builder. Kaniko builds inside an unprivileged pod in userspace; BuildKit can run rootless as a shared, cached build service that jobs connect to over `tcp://`; or build outside the cluster on a hosted runner. `docker buildx` with a remote driver keeps the daemon off the workload node entirely.
- Reading container metadata for a monitoring or service-discovery agent — use a socket proxy that whitelists specific read-only API endpoints (there are purpose-built images for this), mounted read-only, on an internal network. Or in Kubernetes, use the API server with a scoped ServiceAccount instead.
- Docker-in-Docker for tests — prefer a rootless dind sidecar with its own isolated daemon over sharing the host's, and accept the performance cost. Testcontainers-style workflows can also point at a remote daemon.
- Node debugging — `crictl`/`nerdctl` over SSH with proper auditing, not a container with the socket.

And if you must expose the socket at all, the mitigations are: mount it read-only (which does not prevent API writes, so it is weak), use a proxy that filters endpoints, run the daemon rootless so an escape lands as an unprivileged user, and put the whole thing behind admission policy that forbids `hostPath` mounts of the socket in the first place. That last one is the real control: this should be impossible by policy, not avoided by convention.
