How would you let a CI job build images inside a Kubernetes cluster with no socket and no privileged pods?
Does mounting the socket read-only help?

interviewQA.q: How do you handle secrets with Docker — at build time and at run time?
interviewQA.a:
They are two different problems with two different answers, and conflating them is where leaks come from.

Build time. The wrong answers are `ARG` and `ENV`. An `ARG` passed with `--build-arg` is recorded in the image's build metadata and shows up in `docker history` forever; an `ENV` value is in the image config and visible to anyone who can pull the image via `docker inspect`. And `COPY secret . && RUN rm secret` does nothing useful, because layers are immutable diffs — the delete only adds a whiteout while the original bytes stay in the earlier layer blob, recoverable with `docker save` and `tar`.

The right answer is a BuildKit secret mount: `RUN --mount=type=secret,id=npmrc,target=/root/.npmrc npm ci`, built with `docker build --secret id=npmrc,src=$HOME/.npmrc .` (or `,env=TOKEN`). The secret is mounted from a tmpfs for the duration of that one command and appears in no layer, no history and no metadata. For private Git dependencies, `--mount=type=ssh` with `docker build --ssh default` forwards your agent without the key ever entering the build. The multi-stage fallback also works: use the secret in a builder stage and copy only the artefact out, discarding the entire stage.

Run time. Environment variables are the common choice and are acceptable but leaky: they appear in `docker inspect`, in `/proc/<pid>/environ` (readable by anything that can read that process), are inherited by every child process, and get captured by crash reporters and log dumps far more often than people expect. The better pattern is a file, mounted as a tmpfs so it never touches disk, with the application reading it at startup — which is why so many official images support the `_FILE` convention (`POSTGRES_PASSWORD_FILE=/run/secrets/db_password`). Docker Swarm and Compose `secrets:` do exactly this, mounting the value at `/run/secrets/<name>`. Kubernetes Secrets mount as a tmpfs volume the same way, though note they are only base64-encoded in etcd unless you enable encryption at rest, and that RBAC on secrets is what actually protects them.

The mature answer goes one step further: do not store long-lived secrets at all. Use short-lived credentials issued to a workload identity — IAM roles for service accounts on EKS, workload identity on GKE, Vault with a Kubernetes auth backend, or SPIFFE/SPIRE — so the container authenticates as itself and receives a credential that expires in minutes. Then a leak has a bounded blast radius and rotation is automatic rather than a project. And whatever you choose, the operational requirements are the same: a rotation path you have actually exercised, audit logging on secret access, and scanning (`trivy image --scanners secret`, or a pre-commit hook) so a hardcoded key never reaches a registry in the first place.

If a secret has already shipped in an image, the only real remediation is to rotate it. Deleting the tag does not un-pull the image from anyone who already has it.
followUps: Why is `ARG` not a safe way to pass a build-time token?
What are the concrete downsides of passing secrets as environment variables at run time?
What does 'workload identity' buy you over a stored secret?

interviewQA.q: How would you debug a container that has no shell — a distroless or scratch image — in production?
interviewQA.a:
The key insight is that a container is just a namespaced process, so you do not need tools inside the image — you attach a second, tool-bearing process to the same namespaces.

In Kubernetes, the first-class answer is an ephemeral debug container: `kubectl debug -it pod/api-7d9f --image=nicolaka/netshoot --target=api -- bash`. This injects a new container into the running pod sharing the target's namespaces, without restarting anything and without changing the pod spec. From there you have `ss`, `dig`, `tcpdump`, `curl`, `strace` and `mtr`, and — the part people miss — you can read the target's filesystem at `/proc/1/root/` and its environment at `/proc/1/environ`. `kubectl debug node/<node>` gives you a privileged pod on the node itself with the host filesystem at `/host`.

Locally with Docker, the same trick: `docker run --rm -it --pid=container:app --network=container:app --cap-add=SYS_PTRACE --cap-add=NET_ADMIN nicolaka/netshoot`. Sharing the PID namespace makes the target's processes visible and `/proc/1/root/` browsable; sharing the network namespace means `tcpdump` and `ss` see exactly what the app sees.

From the host, no extra container needed: `nsenter -t <pid> -n ss -lntp` for its sockets, `ls -l /proc/<pid>/root/` for its filesystem, `cat /proc/<pid>/environ | tr '\0' '\n'` for its environment, and `/proc/<pid>/cgroup` plus the cgroup files for its real limits and throttling counters.

Without running it at all: `docker create` followed by `docker export | tar -tv` lists every file in the image, and `docker run --rm --entrypoint ls myimage -l /app` overrides the entrypoint to inspect paths. `docker inspect` tells you the configured entrypoint, cmd, user, workdir and env, which resolves a surprising share of "it won't start" cases on its own.

The fallback is the `:debug` tag — most distroless images publish one with a busybox shell — deployed temporarily. I would treat that as a last resort, because it means redeploying and possibly losing the state you were trying to inspect.

I would also mention the preventive side, since that is usually what the interviewer is really probing: build good observability in so you rarely need a shell. Structured logs to stdout, a metrics endpoint, distributed tracing, and a `/debug` endpoint (Go's `net/http/pprof`, for example) give you heap profiles, goroutine dumps and CPU profiles over HTTP from a container with no shell at all. The teams that find distroless painful are usually the ones relying on `exec`-and-poke as their primary debugging strategy.
followUps: What does `--pid=container:x` give you that `--network=container:x` doesn't?
How do you inspect an image's filesystem without running it?
What would you build into the application so you need this less often?

interviewQA.q: Your Docker builds are slow in CI but fast locally. Why, and how do you fix it?
interviewQA.a:
Almost always because the CI runner is ephemeral and has no layer cache, while your laptop has months of accumulated layers. Everything else is secondary but worth checking.

The fix is an exported cache. With buildx: `--cache-from type=registry,ref=ghcr.io/org/app:buildcache` and `--cache-to type=registry,ref=ghcr.io/org/app:buildcache,mode=max`. `mode=max` is the flag that matters — the default `min` exports only the final stage's layers, so in a multi-stage build the expensive build stage is never cached. On GitHub Actions, `type=gha` uses the Actions cache backend; `type=local` with a cached directory and `type=s3` are the other common backends. `type=inline` is cheap and needs no separate storage, but it only covers the final stage.

Then, layered on top, BuildKit cache mounts: `RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.npm` (or `/go/pkg/mod`, `~/.cache/pip`, `~/.m2`, `~/.cargo/registry`). These persist across builds on the same builder without entering any layer, so even when the lockfile genuinely changed and the layer cache correctly missed, you are re-linking rather than re-downloading the world. Note that cache mounts are tied to a builder instance, so with fully ephemeral runners you also need a persistent or remote builder for them to help — a `docker-container` builder on a long-lived machine, or a `kubernetes`/`remote` driver pointing at a shared BuildKit deployment. A shared remote builder is often the single biggest win for a monorepo.

Beyond caching, check these in order:
- Instruction ordering. If `COPY . .` precedes the dependency install, every commit reinstalls everything. Dependency manifests first, install, then source.
- `.dockerignore`. Watch the "transferring context" line in `--progress=plain`. A context of hundreds of MB (usually `.git` and `node_modules`) costs time before the first step runs and changes the `COPY` checksum constantly, so it destroys cache hits too.
- Multi-arch under QEMU. Building `linux/arm64` on an amd64 runner through binfmt emulation can be 5-20x slower for compiled languages. Use native builders — one real machine per architecture, merged by buildx — or restrict which branches build multi-arch.
- Parallelism you are not using. BuildKit runs independent stages concurrently and skips stages the target does not need; a linear Dockerfile written for the legacy builder leaves that on the table. `docker buildx bake` parallelises across multiple images in a monorepo.
- Runner size. Builds are frequently I/O- and CPU-bound; a larger runner is sometimes the cheapest fix available.

And measure rather than guess: `docker build --progress=plain` prints `CACHED` per step, so you can see precisely where the chain broke, and comparing that between a local and a CI run usually identifies the culprit in one pass.
followUps: What does `mode=max` change, and why does it matter for multi-stage builds?
Cache mounts persist across builds — what could go wrong with that?
How would you speed up multi-arch builds without native hardware?

interviewQA.q: How do containers change how you think about application configuration and state?
interviewQA.a:
The core shift is that the image is immutable and environment-agnostic, and everything that differs between environments arrives at run time. One image built once in CI is promoted unchanged from staging to production; if you rebuild per environment, you are testing a different artefact from the one you ship, and the whole idea collapses.

Practically that means: configuration comes from the environment, not from files baked into the image. Environment variables for simple values, mounted files (ConfigMaps, Compose configs, a mounted YAML) for larger ones, and secrets through a secrets mechanism rather than either. No `config.production.yaml` selected by a build argument. An entrypoint script that renders a template from environment variables at startup is a reasonable bridge for software that insists on a config file.

State goes outside the container. The writable layer is deleted with the container and slow to write to because of overlay copy-up, so anything durable belongs on a volume or, better, in an external service — a database, an object store, a cache. Session state in process memory means you cannot scale horizontally or restart safely. Uploaded files on local disk means the next deployment loses them. Application logs written to files means they vanish with the container and never reach your pipeline; write to stdout/stderr and let the platform collect them.

The process must be disposable. It should start fast and handle SIGTERM by draining gracefully, because it will be killed constantly — deployments, scale-downs, node maintenance, spot interruptions, rescheduling. It must tolerate its dependencies not being ready yet and retry rather than crash, because start ordering is not guaranteed in any real orchestrator. And it should be idempotent enough that being started twice or killed mid-work does not corrupt anything, which usually means moving to at-least-once processing with idempotent handlers.

Identity is not stable. IPs and hostnames change on every restart, so service discovery must be name-based (DNS) rather than address-based, and anything that pins to a hostname or writes host-specific state breaks.

Much of this is the Twelve-Factor App, and it is worth naming — but the honest framing is that containers do not invent these constraints, they enforce them. An application that already treated configuration as environment and kept state in a database containerises in an afternoon. One that writes to local disk, holds session state in memory, reads a config file baked next to the binary and needs a 90-second startup will fight the model at every step, and the containerisation project turns into an application-architecture project. Recognising that early — and saying so — is usually what the interviewer is listening for.

flashcards.front: What is a container, in one sentence?
flashcards.back: An ordinary host process with namespaced views of kernel resources (PID, mount, net, UTS, IPC, cgroup), cgroup-enforced resource limits, a reduced capability/syscall set, and a root filesystem assembled from image layers. There is no `struct container` in the kernel.

flashcards.front: Namespaces vs cgroups — one line each
flashcards.back: Namespaces control what a process can SEE (isolation of a kernel resource view). Cgroups control what it can USE (accounting and limits on memory, CPU, I/O, PIDs). Separate subsystems with completely different failure modes.

flashcards.front: Name the Linux namespace types
flashcards.back: mnt, uts, ipc, pid, net, user, cgroup, and time (5.6+). Docker enables all but user and time by default.

flashcards.front: Which namespace does Docker NOT enable by default, and why does it matter?
flashcards.back: The user namespace. Without it, UID 0 in the container is UID 0 on the host — capabilities are dropped and seccomp applies, but any escape lands as real root. Opt in via daemon userns-remap or rootless Docker.

flashcards.front: Why does `nproc` inside a container show the host's CPU count?
flashcards.back: /proc/cpuinfo and /proc/meminfo are not namespaced — there is no 'cpu namespace'. Limits live in cgroup files elsewhere, so runtimes must be told explicitly: GOMAXPROCS, -XX:MaxRAMPercentage, --max-old-space-size.

flashcards.front: pivot_root vs chroot — why do runtimes use pivot_root?
flashcards.back: chroot only changes path resolution and is escapable by a process holding a descriptor to a directory outside it. pivot_root moves the old root away so it can be unmounted, leaving nothing to escape to.

flashcards.front: What does `--cpus=1.5` actually write to the kernel?
flashcards.back: cgroup v2 `cpu.max` = "150000 100000": 150 ms of CPU time per 100 ms period. A hard cap. Exceeding it means throttling, not an error.

flashcards.front: cpu.weight vs cpu.max
flashcards.back: cpu.weight (v1: cpu.shares, Docker --cpu-shares) is a RELATIVE priority applied only under contention — an uncontended low-weight group can use the whole machine. cpu.max (Docker --cpus) is a HARD quota-per-period cap that throttles.

flashcards.front: Exit code 137 — what does it mean and what are the two causes?
flashcards.back: 128 + 9 = SIGKILL. Either the cgroup OOM killer (check `docker inspect -f '{{.State.OOMKilled}}'` and dmesg) or `docker stop`'s grace period expiring because PID 1 ignored SIGTERM.

flashcards.front: Exit codes 125, 126, 127
flashcards.back: 125 = the docker daemon/command itself failed (bad flag, bad mount, port in use). 126 = command found but not executable. 127 = command not found — on scratch/distroless this usually means a missing dynamic loader for a non-static binary.

flashcards.front: Why is `docker stats` memory misleading?
flashcards.back: It includes reclaimable page cache. A container that only READ a 2 GB file shows 2 GB. Alert on `anon` in memory.stat, or on container_memory_working_set_bytes — not container_memory_usage_bytes.

flashcards.front: How do you detect CPU throttling, and why does average CPU hide it?
flashcards.back: Read nr_throttled and throttled_usec in cpu.stat (Prometheus: container_cpu_cfs_throttled_seconds_total). Many threads can burn the whole quota in the first 10 ms of a 100 ms period, freezing the app for 90 ms while average utilisation reads ~10-40%.

flashcards.front: Image vs container
flashcards.back: An image is a read-only ordered stack of layers plus a config blob. A container is an instance of that image with one thin writable layer on top. Class vs object. `docker rm` deletes only the writable layer.

flashcards.front: Image ID vs repo digest
flashcards.back: Image ID (in `docker images`) = SHA-256 of the CONFIG blob. Repo digest (`app@sha256:...`, what you pin) = SHA-256 of the MANIFEST. Different hashes for the same image.

flashcards.front: What is a whiteout file?
flashcards.back: How OverlayFS marks a file deleted when it exists in an immutable lower layer: a char device 0/0 in the upper layer (or a `.wh.<name>` entry in the OCI tar format). The original bytes remain in the lower layer blob.

flashcards.front: Does `RUN rm secret.json` remove the secret from an image?
flashcards.back: No. It adds a whiteout in a new layer; the bytes stay in the earlier layer and are extractable with `docker save`. The image also gets bigger. Fix: `RUN --mount=type=secret`, or a multi-stage build that discards the stage.

flashcards.front: What is copy-up in OverlayFS?
flashcards.back: The first write to a file from a read-only lower layer copies the ENTIRE file into the writable upper layer first. Appending one byte to a 2 GB file costs a 2 GB copy — which is why write-heavy paths must be on a volume.

flashcards.front: The Docker build cache key — what goes into it?
flashcards.back: The parent layer's identity plus the instruction text; for COPY/ADD, plus a checksum of the file contents. A miss invalidates every subsequent instruction and never recovers, so order least-changing to most-changing.

flashcards.front: Why must `apt-get update` and `apt-get install` be one RUN?
flashcards.back: Only the command STRING is hashed for RUN. A separate `apt-get update` hits the cache forever, serving a stale index, and the later install 404s on package versions the mirror has dropped.

flashcards.front: The single most impactful Dockerfile layering change
flashcards.back: Copy dependency manifests, install, THEN copy source. `COPY package.json && npm ci && COPY . .` instead of `COPY . . && npm ci` — dependency install stops re-running on every commit.

flashcards.front: What does `.dockerignore` prevent?
flashcards.back: Shipping .git/node_modules/.env into the context and the image (size, secrets, wrong-platform binaries shadowing installed ones) and constant COPY cache invalidation because those directories change on every commit.

flashcards.front: COPY vs ADD
flashcards.back: Use COPY. ADD additionally auto-extracts LOCAL tar archives and can fetch remote URLs (which it does not extract) — surprising behaviour. Only use ADD for deliberate tar extraction or `ADD --checksum=` verified fetches.

flashcards.front: ARG vs ENV — and are either secret?
flashcards.back: ARG is build-time only and absent from the final image environment; ENV is baked into the image config. NEITHER is secret: ARG appears in `docker history`, ENV in `docker inspect`. Use `RUN --mount=type=secret`.

flashcards.front: ENTRYPOINT + CMD — what runs?
flashcards.back: ENTRYPOINT with CMD appended as arguments. `docker run img args` replaces CMD only; `--entrypoint` replaces the entrypoint. Setting ENTRYPOINT resets an inherited CMD to empty.

flashcards.front: Why is shell-form CMD a production bug?
flashcards.back: `CMD python app.py` becomes `/bin/sh -c "python app.py"`, making sh PID 1. SIGTERM from `docker stop` hits the shell, which does not forward it; the app never drains and is SIGKILLed after 10 s (exit 137). Use exec form.

flashcards.front: What is special about PID 1 in a PID namespace?
flashcards.back: (1) Signals other than SIGKILL/SIGSTOP with no installed handler are DISCARDED, so SIGTERM does nothing to a naive PID 1. (2) Orphans reparent to it and it must reap them or zombies exhaust PIDs. (3) If PID 1 exits, the whole namespace dies.

flashcards.front: What does `docker run --init` do?
flashcards.back: Inserts tini as PID 1, which forwards signals to your process and reaps orphaned children. Needed when PID 1 is a shell script, a supervisor, or a runtime that abandons children.

flashcards.front: Why must an entrypoint script end with `exec "$@"`?
flashcards.back: `exec` REPLACES the shell with your process, so your app becomes PID 1 and receives SIGTERM directly. Without it the shell stays as PID 1, the signal stops there, and graceful shutdown never happens.

flashcards.front: What is `docker stop`'s contract?
flashcards.back: Send STOPSIGNAL (default SIGTERM) to PID 1, wait `-t` seconds (default 10), then SIGKILL. Your process should stop accepting work, fail readiness, drain in-flight requests, and exit 0.

flashcards.front: What does a multi-stage build give you, in priority order?
flashcards.back: Security (no compiler, no package manager, no build-time credentials in the final image), size (Go: 850 MB -> under 15 MB), and maintainability (one file, build and runtime versioned together). Only the last stage ships.

flashcards.front: What does `--target` do in a multi-stage build?
flashcards.back: Builds a specific named stage. Enables `--target=dev` (with tooling), `--target=test` (runs the suite, gating CI), and `--target=prod` from one Dockerfile. BuildKit skips stages the target does not depend on.

flashcards.front: Four things `FROM scratch` is missing that you must supply
flashcards.back: CA certificates (else x509 unknown authority on every HTTPS call), /etc/passwd (for a named USER), /usr/share/zoneinfo (else TZ silently does nothing), and /tmp. Plus the binary must be statically linked.

flashcards.front: Why `CGO_ENABLED=0` for Go on scratch/distroless-static?
flashcards.back: By default net and os/user use cgo to call glibc NSS, producing a dynamically linked binary. CGO_ENABLED=0 selects the pure-Go resolvers and yields a truly static binary.

flashcards.front: "no such file or directory" running a binary that clearly exists — what is it?
flashcards.back: The dynamic LOADER is missing (e.g. /lib64/ld-linux-x86-64.so.2 absent from scratch, or a glibc binary on musl/Alpine). Confirm with `ldd`. Fix: build static, or match the runtime libc to the build libc.

flashcards.front: What is distroless and what is the tradeoff?
flashcards.back: glibc + CA certs + tzdata + /etc/passwd, but no shell, no package manager, no coreutils. Near-zero OS-package CVEs and a tiny attack surface; the cost is that `docker exec sh` does not work, so you debug via a sidecar sharing the namespaces.

flashcards.front: Why is Alpine often the wrong base for Python?
flashcards.back: musl libc means PyPI's manylinux wheels do not install, so pip compiles from source: builds go from ~30 s to ~15 min, need a toolchain, and the result is often LARGER than python:3.12-slim. Also musl DNS and thread-stack differences.

flashcards.front: Named volume vs bind mount — the two behavioural differences
flashcards.back: A named volume is Docker-managed and, if empty on first use, is SEEDED with the image's content at that path. A bind mount takes whatever is on the host and SHADOWS the image content (an empty host dir hides the image's files).

flashcards.front: Why `--mount` over `-v`?
flashcards.back: With `-v`, a nonexistent bind source is silently created as an empty root-owned directory, so a typo produces a mystery instead of an error. `--mount type=bind` fails loudly, and its key=value syntax is explicit.

flashcards.front: Why does a container get 'permission denied' on a bind mount?
flashcards.back: The kernel compares numeric UID/GID and there is no translation across the boundary. Align the numbers (`--user $(id -u):$(id -g)` or chown the host dir), do not chmod 777. On SELinux hosts also add `:z` or `:Z`.

flashcards.front: What is the trap with tmpfs mounts?
flashcards.back: tmpfs pages are charged to the container's MEMORY cgroup. `--memory=256m` plus 300 MB written to /tmp or /dev/shm = OOM kill, exit 137. Same applies to Docker's 64 MB default /dev/shm being too small for Postgres/Chrome.

flashcards.front: Why is `VOLUME` in a Dockerfile usually a mistake?
flashcards.back: It creates a new ANONYMOUS volume on every `docker run` that nobody cleans up, and any RUN after it that writes to that path has its changes silently discarded. Let the operator choose mounts at run time.

flashcards.front: Default bridge vs user-defined bridge
flashcards.back: A user-defined bridge gets Docker's embedded DNS at 127.0.0.11 resolving container names and aliases; the default docker0 does NOT (only the deprecated --link). User-defined bridges are also isolated from each other. Compose creates one per project.

flashcards.front: What does `-p 8080:80` install?
flashcards.back: A DNAT rule in the nat table's DOCKER chain rewriting destination host:8080 to container-ip:80, plus a docker-proxy process for loopback/hairpin cases. Egress separately gets a MASQUERADE rule in nat POSTROUTING.

flashcards.front: Why did publishing a port bypass my ufw rules?
flashcards.back: Docker's DNAT runs in nat/PREROUTING and the packet then traverses FORWARD — it never reaches filter/INPUT where ufw's rules live. Fix: `-p 127.0.0.1:port:port`, bind a private interface, or filter in the DOCKER-USER chain.

flashcards.front: EXPOSE — what does it actually do?
flashcards.back: Nothing at run time. It is metadata that `docker run -P` and some tooling read. Ports are reachable only via `-p`/`--publish` or an orchestrator's port mapping.

flashcards.front: How does `--network=container:x` relate to Kubernetes?
flashcards.back: It joins an existing container's network namespace so both share interfaces and localhost. That is exactly how a Pod works: a sandbox ('pause') container owns the netns and every container joins it — hence one IP per pod and localhost communication.

flashcards.front: Overlay network MTU trap
flashcards.back: VXLAN adds ~50 bytes of header, so effective MTU drops to ~1450. Leave it at 1500 and handshakes plus small requests work while large responses hang — full-size segments are dropped, especially where blocked ICMP breaks PMTUD.

flashcards.front: Why doesn't `depends_on` in Compose fix startup ordering?
flashcards.back: By default it only waits for the container to START, not to be READY. Add a healthcheck to the dependency and `depends_on: { db: { condition: service_healthy } }`. Conditions: service_started, service_healthy, service_completed_successfully.

flashcards.front: Compose `.env` file vs `env_file:`
flashcards.back: `.env` supplies values for ${VAR} INTERPOLATION inside the compose file (it configures Compose). `env_file:` lists files whose contents become ENVIRONMENT VARIABLES INSIDE the container (it configures the app). Unrelated mechanisms.

flashcards.front: Tag vs digest
flashcards.back: A tag is a MUTABLE pointer that anyone with push access can reassign; a digest (`app@sha256:...`) is the immutable content hash of the manifest. Build with an immutable tag, DEPLOY BY DIGEST. `latest` has no notion of recency.

flashcards.front: What is an image index / manifest list?
flashcards.back: A manifest whose entries are other manifests, each annotated with os/architecture/variant. It is how one tag serves arm64 on an M-series Mac and amd64 in CI. Inspect with `docker buildx imagetools inspect`.

flashcards.front: "exec format error" — cause?
flashcards.back: Architecture mismatch (an amd64 image on arm64 hardware, common when building on Apple Silicon for x86 nodes), or a script with a missing/incorrect shebang, or CRLF line endings making the kernel look for `/bin/sh\r`.

flashcards.front: How does a registry push work?
flashcards.back: HEAD each blob digest to see what the registry already has, POST/PATCH/PUT to upload only the missing blobs, then PUT the manifest LAST. That ordering is why an interrupted push never leaves a half-visible image.

flashcards.front: How does registry auth work?
flashcards.back: The registry replies 401 with `WWW-Authenticate: Bearer realm=...,service=...,scope=...`; the client fetches a short-lived scoped token from that realm and retries. `docker login` stores credentials base64-encoded (NOT encrypted) in ~/.docker/config.json.

flashcards.front: What does `RUN --mount=type=cache` do?
flashcards.back: Mounts a directory that persists ACROSS builds but enters no layer — the right home for ~/.npm, /go/pkg/mod, ~/.cache/pip, ~/.m2. Keeps downloads warm even when the lockfile changed, at zero image-size cost. Tied to a builder instance.

flashcards.front: How do you use a private token in a build without leaking it?
flashcards.back: `RUN --mount=type=secret,id=tok,target=/root/.npmrc ...` with `docker build --secret id=tok,src=...` (or `,env=VAR`). Mounted from tmpfs for one command; in no layer, no history, no metadata. For git: `--mount=type=ssh` with `--ssh default`.

flashcards.front: What does `# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1` buy you?
flashcards.back: BuildKit fetches that Dockerfile frontend image to parse the file, so new syntax (cache/secret/ssh mounts, COPY --link, heredocs) works without upgrading Docker itself. Put it on line 1 of every Dockerfile.

flashcards.front: What does `mode=max` change on a registry cache export?
flashcards.back: It exports intermediate stage layers too, not just the final stage's — which is what makes a multi-stage build actually cacheable on ephemeral CI runners.

flashcards.front: Name the stack behind `docker run`
flashcards.back: docker CLI -> (HTTP over /var/run/docker.sock) dockerd -> (gRPC) containerd -> containerd-shim-runc-v2 (one per container, stays alive) -> runc (sets up namespaces/cgroups/mounts, execs, then EXITS).

flashcards.front: Why does restarting dockerd not kill running containers?
flashcards.back: Each container's parent is its containerd-shim, not dockerd. The shim holds the stdio/pty and reports exit status, so the daemon can restart or upgrade and reattach. Enable `live-restore` on non-Swarm hosts.

flashcards.front: The three OCI specifications
flashcards.back: Image spec (manifests, configs, layers), Runtime spec (the bundle: rootfs + config.json, and create/start/kill/delete), Distribution spec (the registry HTTP API). These are what make runc/crun/gVisor and containerd/CRI-O interchangeable.

flashcards.front: Kubernetes removed dockershim in 1.24 — what actually changed?
flashcards.back: The kubelet calls containerd/CRI-O directly through the CRI instead of going via dockerd. Your OCI images are unaffected. What broke: mounting the docker socket to build images, `docker ps` for node debugging (use crictl/nerdctl), and Docker-JSON log parsers.

flashcards.front: Why is mounting /var/run/docker.sock equivalent to giving out host root?
flashcards.back: It is the full Engine API with no authorisation. One command starts a --privileged container with / mounted and chroots into it. Use Kaniko, rootless BuildKit, or a filtering socket proxy instead.

flashcards.front: Docker's default capability set
flashcards.back: 14 of ~40 are kept: CHOWN, DAC_OVERRIDE, FOWNER, FSETID, KILL, SETGID, SETUID, SETPCAP, NET_BIND_SERVICE, NET_RAW, SYS_CHROOT, MKNOD, AUDIT_WRITE, SETFCAP. Harden with `--cap-drop=ALL` and add back only what is needed.

flashcards.front: What does `--privileged` actually disable?
flashcards.back: Grants all capabilities, disables the seccomp and AppArmor profiles, and exposes host devices. Effectively only the mount namespace remains, and that is trivially crossed. Never use it for application workloads.

flashcards.front: What is `no-new-privileges`?
flashcards.back: `--security-opt=no-new-privileges` sets PR_SET_NO_NEW_PRIVS so execve cannot grant additional privileges — setuid binaries stop escalating. Cheap, and it blocks a whole class of escalation from a compromised non-root process.

flashcards.front: Why numeric UID in `USER`?
flashcards.back: Kubernetes' `runAsNonRoot: true` reads the image config and cannot verify that a USERNAME is non-root, so a name-only USER fails admission. `USER 10001` is verifiable. Also: non-root cannot bind ports below 1024 — listen on 8080.

flashcards.front: What do vulnerability scanners actually read?
flashcards.back: Package databases (/var/lib/dpkg/status, RPM DB, /lib/apk/db/installed) plus language lockfiles, matched against CVE feeds. They MISS anything curl'ed or built from source, statically linked C libs, and your own code's bugs.

flashcards.front: The highest-leverage vulnerability control
flashcards.back: Rebuilding regularly. Most findings are fixed by a newer base image, not by any change to your code, so an automated weekly rebuild-and-redeploy of unchanged services removes more risk than most scanning policies.

flashcards.front: What is an SBOM for?
flashcards.back: An inventory (SPDX/CycloneDX) of everything in an image, so the next Log4Shell is a query against 400 recorded manifests instead of rebuilding and rescanning 400 images. Generate with `docker buildx build --sbom=true` or `trivy image --format cyclonedx`.

flashcards.front: Keyless signing with cosign — what does it avoid?
flashcards.back: Key management. The signature binds to a short-lived certificate issued to your CI's OIDC identity and is recorded in the Rekor transparency log. Verify with `--certificate-identity-regexp` and `--certificate-oidc-issuer`, and enforce via admission policy.

flashcards.front: Why must you configure Docker log rotation?
flashcards.back: The default json-file driver has NO size limit. A crash-looping chatty service fills /var/lib/docker and then everything on the host fails. Set max-size/max-file in daemon.json — it applies only to newly created containers.

flashcards.front: What breaks when you switch off the json-file log driver?
flashcards.back: `docker logs` returns nothing — with awslogs/gcplogs/fluentd/splunk the daemon keeps no local copy. Also, json-file is blocking by default; use `mode=non-blocking` so a stalled log sink cannot stall your application.

flashcards.front: Liveness vs readiness probe
flashcards.back: Liveness failing RESTARTS the container, so it must only test 'am I wedged' — never a dependency, or one slow database minute restarts the fleet. Readiness failing removes the pod from Service endpoints without restarting; dependency checks belong there.

flashcards.front: Does Docker restart an unhealthy container?
flashcards.back: No. HEALTHCHECK sets the status and emits events; plain Docker takes no action. Swarm restarts on it, Compose gates `depends_on` on it, and Kubernetes ignores it entirely in favour of its own probes.

flashcards.front: Docker restart policies
flashcards.back: `no` (default), `on-failure[:N]` (non-zero exit only), `always` (including after daemon restart/reboot), `unless-stopped` (like always but respects a manual stop across restarts). Backoff is exponential from 100 ms — the same idea as CrashLoopBackOff.

flashcards.front: Four places containers fill a disk
flashcards.back: Images, the BuildKit cache (`docker buildx prune` — often tens of GB and the actual culprit), volumes, and logs. `docker image prune` only touches the first. `docker system df -v` shows all four.

flashcards.front: How do you debug a container with no shell?
flashcards.back: Attach a second process to its namespaces: `kubectl debug --target=app --image=nicolaka/netshoot`, or `docker run --pid=container:app --network=container:app netshoot`, or `nsenter` from the host. Read the target's files at /proc/1/root/.

flashcards.front: Fastest first three commands when a container will not start
flashcards.back: `docker logs --tail=200 `; `docker inspect --format '{{.State.ExitCode}} {{.State.OOMKilled}} {{.State.Error}}'`; `docker inspect --format '{{.Config.Entrypoint}} {{.Config.Cmd}} {{.Config.User}}'`. Exit code tells you which branch to walk.

flashcards.front: Published port refused but the app is running — first check?
flashcards.back: What address the process bound to. `127.0.0.1:8080` inside the container is unreachable through a DNAT rule; it must bind `0.0.0.0:8080`. Confirm with `docker exec <c> ss -lntp`.

flashcards.front: Why must containerised apps log to stdout/stderr?
flashcards.back: Files in the writable layer vanish with the container and never reach the log pipeline. The platform collects stdout/stderr. For software that insists on files, symlink them to /dev/stdout and /dev/stderr, as the official nginx image does.
